ana-emb-sa-h-1.why: The sinus venosus forms the caudal inflow end of the straight heart tube. It receives the embryonic venous return and passes it into the primitive atrium.

notes.A: The primitive atrium receives blood from the sinus venosus, placing it just beyond the venous inlet.
notes.B: The bulbus cordis lies at the arterial end and contributes to the developing right ventricle.
notes.D: The primitive ventricle lies between the atrium and bulbus cordis and pumps blood towards the arterial end.
notes.E: The similarly named conus cordis forms ventricular outflow tracts at the arterial end of the tube.

ana-emb-sa-h-2.why: The free margin of the septum secundum forms the rim of the foramen ovale. The thinner septum primum overlaps the opening on its left side and acts as its valve.

notes.A: The thin septum primum supplies the mobile flap that covers the opening on its left side.
notes.B: The septum spurium forms where the venous valves meet near the entry of the sinus venosus.
notes.D: The venous valves form the septum spurium, whereas the rim of the opening belongs to the septum secundum.
notes.E: The septum secundum leaves an identifiable opening through which foetal blood passes into the left atrium.

ana-emb-sa-h-3.why: The ductus venosus carries a portion of the relatively oxygen-rich blood from the left umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic sinusoids.

notes.A: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta so blood can bypass the foetal lungs.
notes.B: The truncus arteriosus is the common arterial outlet of the embryonic heart before the great arteries separate.
notes.C: The sinus venosus receives embryonic venous blood at the heart and has no direct shunting role within the liver.
notes.E: The ductus venosus provides the named connection that allows placental blood to bypass much of the hepatic circulation.

ana-emb-sa-h-9.why: The dorsal and ventral atrioventricular endocardial cushions fuse in the common canal. The resulting septum intermedium separates the canal into right and left atrioventricular openings.

notes.A: The foramen ovale is a passage between the foetal atria, above the level of the atrioventricular canal.
notes.B: The septum secundum forms the rim of the interatrial opening on the right side of the atrial septum.
notes.C: The septum spurium arises near the venous inlet from the upper ends of the venous valves.
notes.D: The septum primum grows from the atrial roof towards the cushions and helps partition the atria.

ana-emb-sa-h-10.why: Displacement of the outlet septum produces an overriding aorta, a ventricular septal defect and right ventricular outflow obstruction. The increased right ventricular pressure load leads to hypertrophy.

notes.B: The aorta overrides the septal defect, allowing it to receive blood from both ventricles.
notes.C: Displacement of the outlet septum leaves a gap between the ventricles immediately beneath the overriding aorta.
notes.D: The displaced outlet septum narrows the right ventricular outflow tract, restricting flow towards the lungs.
notes.E: The right ventricular muscle becomes hypertrophied as it pumps against the obstruction at its outlet.

ana-emb-sa-h-74-77.why: The umbilical vein brings placental blood to the foetus. Preferential streaming across the foramen ovale helps supply the heart and upper body with relatively well-oxygenated arterial blood.

notes.A: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood towards the foetus, while the paired umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.
notes.C: Among the systemic arteries, the ascending aorta and its arch branches receive relatively oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle.
notes.B: High resistance in the foetal lungs favours flow from the pulmonary artery into the descending aorta through the ductus arteriosus.

ana-emb-sa-h-78-82.why: Overlapping atrial septa create an oblique right-to-left passage. Once pulmonary venous return increases at birth, higher left atrial pressure holds the flexible septum primum against the rim.

notes.A: The septum primum grows from the roof of the common atrium towards the endocardial cushions.
notes.B: The septum secundum develops to the right of the septum primum and overlaps its opening.
notes.C: The openings in the overlapping septa are offset, producing an oblique route from the right atrium to the left.
notes.D: The flexible septum primum opens like a flap against the more substantial septum secundum.
notes.E: Lung aeration increases pulmonary blood flow and left atrial pressure. Functional closure occurs when left pressure exceeds right, and anatomical fusion can lag or remain incomplete.

ana-emb-sa-h-83-90.why: Expansion of the ventricular chambers produces the muscular septum and initially leaves an interventricular opening. The cushions and neighbouring outflow tissues help close the remaining gap.

notes.A: Looping positions the cardiac chambers, whereas growth of the ventricular myocardium produces the muscular septum.
notes.B: The muscular septum arises at the floor of the developing ventricles as their walls expand.
notes.C: Tissue from the atrioventricular cushions helps close the remaining gap above the muscular septum.
notes.E: The membranous region is a common site of defects because several developing structures must unite there.
notes.D: The primitive ventricle gives rise to the trabeculated portion that forms most of the left ventricle.

ana-emb-sa-h-91-95.why: The outflow tract separates into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Remodelling of the aortic sac and pharyngeal arch arteries then establishes their connections with the great vessels.

notes.A: The third arch forms the common carotid artery and the proximal part of the internal carotid artery on each side.
notes.B: The proximal sixth arch arteries contribute to the pulmonary arteries on their respective sides.
notes.E: The right horn of the aortic sac gives rise to the brachiocephalic trunk.
notes.C: The distal left sixth arch persists as the ductus arteriosus, joining the left pulmonary artery to the descending aorta.
notes.D: Partition of the truncus arteriosus produces the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk.

ana-emb-es-1.why: The intra-abdominal left umbilical vein closes after birth and its fibrous remnant becomes the round ligament of the liver. It runs along the free margin of the falciform ligament.

notes.A: The distal umbilical arteries become the paired medial umbilical ligaments, which run beside the bladder on the anterior abdominal wall.
notes.B: The ductus arteriosus closes and forms the ligamentum arteriosum between the left pulmonary artery and the aortic arch.
notes.C: The ductus venosus closes and forms the ligamentum venosum within the liver, beyond the course of the former umbilical vein.
notes.E: The vitelline veins form parts of the portal venous system and the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava.

ana-emb-es-9.why: The thin septum primum forms the flap on the left side of the foramen ovale. Raising left atrial pressure presses the flap against the stiffer septum secundum.

notes.A: Endocardial cushions help partition the atrioventricular canal, whereas the flap comes from the septum growing down from the atrial roof.
notes.B: The crista dividens is a ridge that separates incoming blood streams at the rim of the interatrial opening.
notes.D: The septum secundum provides the rim against which the thinner flap closes when left atrial pressure rises.
notes.E: The inferior caval valve helps direct blood towards the foramen ovale from the venous inlet upstream of the flap.

ana-emb-es-119.why: Failure of embryonic outflow tract separation leaves one common arterial trunk supplying systemic and pulmonary circulations. It usually overrides a large ventricular septal defect.

notes.A: Tetralogy of Fallot involves an abnormally positioned outlet septum, with pulmonary outflow obstruction and an overriding aorta.
notes.B: In transposition there are two separate great arteries, but each connects to the opposite ventricle.
notes.D: A ventricular septal defect is an opening between the ventricles. It often accompanies a common arterial trunk.
notes.E: A patent ductus arteriosus connects an already separate pulmonary artery and aorta through a persistent foetal vessel.

ana-emb-sa-h-38.why: The laryngotracheal bud grows out from ventral foregut endoderm. Its endoderm forms respiratory epithelium, while surrounding splanchnic mesoderm gives rise to supporting cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue.

notes.A: Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis, whereas the respiratory bud arises within the endoderm-lined foregut.
notes.C: Splanchnic mesoderm around the bud forms bronchial cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue around the endodermal lining.
notes.D: Somatic mesoderm lines the body wall and contributes to the parietal pleura surrounding each lung.
notes.E: Extraembryonic mesoderm supports structures outside the embryo, including placental vessels, whereas the lung bud forms within the embryo.

ana-emb-sa-h-39.why: An affected lobar bronchus can narrow during expiration when its cartilaginous support is inadequate. Trapped air progressively overinflates the lobe and can compress adjacent functional lung.

notes.A: Oligohydramnios can limit lung growth, leaving small lungs with insufficient tissue for gas exchange.
notes.B: Surfactant deficiency increases surface tension and promotes alveolar collapse at the end of expiration.
notes.C: Unilateral agenesis leaves an entire lung absent and cannot account for air trapping within a developing lobe.
notes.E: A tracheo-oesophageal fistula can permit aspiration or gastric distension. An extra lobe alone supplies no mechanism for focal expiratory air trapping.

ana-emb-sa-h-40.why: The ventral respiratory diverticulum normally separates from the dorsal oesophagus during foregut development. Abnormal separation can leave a fistula between the trachea and oesophagus.

notes.B: Congenital lobar overinflation results from expiratory air trapping, sometimes because an affected bronchus lacks adequate cartilage.
notes.C: Congenital lung cysts arise within the developing airways or lung tissue, away from the tracheo-oesophageal partition.
notes.D: Hyaline membrane disease arises when surfactant deficiency allows alveoli to collapse, usually in a premature infant.
notes.E: Accessory lung lobes result from variations in branching or lobulation within the developing lung.

ana-emb-sa-h-142-145.why: An abnormal tract between trachea and oesophagus permits cross-flow. With a distal fistula, airway pressure can inflate the stomach and gastro-oesophageal reflux can enter the airway.

notes.C: Focal lobar overinflation suggests an obstructed bronchus, whereas an open fistula primarily predisposes to aspiration.
notes.A: With a distal fistula, raised airway pressure during crying can drive air through the oesophagus into the stomach.
notes.B: Refluxing gastric contents can travel up the distal oesophagus and through the fistula, causing aspiration and lung injury.
notes.D: Surgical closure separates the airway and digestive tract and prevents continued passage of material through the fistula.

ana-emb-es-91.why: Pleuropericardial folds grow medially and separate the pleural spaces from the pericardial cavity. Their fusion helps form the fibrous pericardial partition around the heart.

notes.B: The pleuroperitoneal folds help close communications between the developing pleural and peritoneal cavities and contribute to the diaphragm.
notes.C: The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart, but the partitions that separate it from the pleural cavities develop as named folds.
notes.D: The dorsal mesentery suspends the developing gut from the posterior body wall within the abdomen.
notes.E: The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm between the thorax and abdomen.

ana-emb-sa-h-11.why: The pectinate line marks the junction between upper anal canal epithelium derived from hindgut endoderm and the lower segment derived from ectoderm of the proctodeum.

notes.B: The epithelium above the pectinate line is derived from hindgut endoderm and is continuous with the rectal lining.
notes.C: The left colic flexure lies at the transition to descending colon within the distal transverse colon and hindgut territory.
notes.D: The descending colon is formed by the hindgut and is supplied by branches of the inferior mesenteric artery.
notes.E: The sigmoid colon forms from distal hindgut and continues into the rectum, another hindgut derivative.

ana-emb-sa-h-12.why: The urorectal septum is the intervening mesenchyme at the cloaca. It separates the ventral urogenital sinus, continuous with the allantois, from the dorsal anorectal canal.

notes.A: The proctodeum is a surface ectodermal depression that contributes the lower anal canal below the pectinate line.
notes.C: The cloaca is the common terminal chamber being partitioned. The dividing wedge is mesenchyme within this region.
notes.D: The perineal body forms at the junction between the future anal and urogenital openings, at the caudal end of the partition.
notes.E: The urogenital membrane covers the ventral opening after partition and later breaks down. It is separate from the mesenchymal wedge.

ana-emb-sa-h-16.why: The buccopharyngeal membrane closes the cranial end of the early foregut. Its breakdown opens a connection between the primitive mouth and the developing pharynx.

notes.A: The yolk sac connects to the midgut through a narrowing stalk. This junction lies caudal to the primitive pharynx.
notes.B: The vitelline duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac. It does not form the cranial limit of the foregut.
notes.C: The cloacal membrane marks the caudal outlet of the hindgut region, at the opposite end of the developing gut tube.
notes.E: The respiratory bud forms from the ventral foregut below the pharynx, caudal to the buccopharyngeal membrane.

ana-emb-sa-h-17.why: The dorsal pancreatic bud arises independently from the dorsal duodenal endoderm. The ventral pancreatic bud, hepatic primordium and gallbladder are associated with the ventral hepatic diverticulum.

notes.B: The ventral pancreatic primordium arises from the ventral foregut near or as part of the developing hepatic diverticulum.
notes.C: The gallbladder develops from the cystic portion of the hepatic diverticulum, caudal to the liver-forming portion.
notes.D: The cystic bud is the portion of the ventral diverticulum that gives rise to the gallbladder and cystic duct.
notes.E: The liver-forming portion of the diverticulum gives rise to hepatic tissue and contributes to the developing biliary tract.

ana-emb-sa-h-19.why: The accessory pancreatic duct can persist from the dorsal pancreatic duct on the minor-papilla side of the fusion point. The rest joins the main duct system.

notes.A: The stalk of the cystic bud forms the cystic duct, which connects the gallbladder to the extrahepatic bile ducts.
notes.B: The common bile duct carries bile and usually joins the main pancreatic duct near the major papilla.
notes.C: The ventral bud duct forms the outlet portion of the main duct at the major duodenal papilla.
notes.E: The common hepatic duct drains the liver. It joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.

ana-emb-sa-h-47.why: A completely patent vitelline duct persists as an ileo-umbilical fistula. Its open connection to the bowel lumen allows intestinal contents to discharge through the umbilicus.

notes.A: Meckel’s diverticulum is a blind pouch persisting at the ileal end. It has no open outlet at the umbilicus.
notes.B: A fibrous remnant can tether the ileum to the umbilicus and predispose to obstruction. It lacks an open lumen.
notes.D: A vitelline sinus has a patent umbilical end but closes towards the bowel, so it has no direct faecal communication.
notes.E: A vitelline duct cyst retains a central portion with closed ends. It has no continuous opening between the ileum and skin.

ana-emb-sa-h-48.why: An omphalocoele is a midline herniation into the umbilical cord, usually contained by an amnion-covered sac. The cord inserts into the sac rather than beside it.

notes.A: Gastroschisis usually lies beside the umbilicus. The bowel has no covering sac and the cord inserts separately.
notes.C: A congenital umbilical hernia protrudes through an umbilical ring beneath skin. It lacks the amnion-covered sac described here.
notes.D: Physiological midgut herniation is normal early in development and resolves before birth as bowel returns to the abdomen.
notes.E: An amnion-covered sac with the cord inserting into it is a characteristic anatomical finding in omphalocoele.

ana-emb-sa-h-103-110.why: The ventral pancreatic bud forms the uncinate process and inferior head. The dorsal bud forms most of the rest, and remodelling of both ducts establishes the definitive drainage pattern.

notes.A: The uncinate process grows from the ventral bud. It hooks behind the superior mesenteric vessels after rotation and fusion.
notes.B: The ventral bud supplies the uncinate process and part of the pancreatic head, particularly its inferior portion.
notes.C: The tail is a dorsal bud derivative and extends towards the spleen as the pancreas develops.
notes.D: The body develops from the dorsal bud along with the tail and part of the head.
notes.E: The main duct segment nearest its duodenal outlet is formed from the ventral bud duct.
notes.F: The body and tail portion of the main duct is formed from the dorsal duct beyond its union with the ventral duct.
notes.G: Persistence of the dorsal duct toward its original duodenal opening can leave an accessory duct at the minor papilla.
notes.H: In one classical model, a bifid ventral bud migrates around both sides of the duodenum and forms a pancreatic ring.

ana-emb-sa-h-111-117.why: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis results from thickening of the pyloric muscle, especially its circular layer. Gastric outlet narrowing leads to forceful non-bilious vomiting, typically after the first weeks of life.

notes.A: Hypertrophy predominantly affects the circular smooth muscle. This narrows the pyloric channel and impedes gastric emptying.
notes.B: The stomach contracts against the narrowed outlet, producing forceful vomiting of gastric contents without bile.
notes.C: Reduced passage of feeds into the intestine can decrease stool output and may lead to constipation.
notes.D: The condition is considerably more frequent in male infants, although it can also occur in females.
notes.E: Increased numbers of autonomic ganglion cells are not the defining change. The characteristic lesion is muscular thickening of the pylorus.
notes.F: After fluid and electrolyte correction, pyloromyotomy relieves the obstruction and is generally effective.
notes.G: Presentation is typical several weeks after birth. Although timing varies, the first three days are unusually early.

ana-emb-es-21.why: The foregut–midgut boundary in the duodenum lies near the major papilla. The proximal duodenum is foregut-derived and chiefly supplied from the coeliac system via pancreaticoduodenal branches.

notes.A: The ileum is part of the midgut and receives branches of the superior mesenteric artery through its mesentery.
notes.B: The jejunum is midgut-derived. Jejunal arteries arise from the superior mesenteric artery and form mesenteric arcades.
notes.C: The caecum develops from the midgut loop and receives blood through the ileocolic branch of the superior mesenteric artery.
notes.D: Distal to the major papilla the duodenum is midgut-derived. Inferior pancreaticoduodenal branches arise from the superior mesenteric artery.

ana-emb-es-22.why: Omphalocoele has a covering sac containing peritoneum and amnion, with the cord attached to it. Gastroschisis leaves the protruding bowel exposed through a separate defect.

notes.B: A defect just to the right of the umbilicus is typical of gastroschisis. Omphalocoele is centred on the umbilical ring.
notes.C: Both conditions involve the anterior abdominal wall. The covering and relation to the cord distinguish them.
notes.D: A separate, normally inserted cord favours gastroschisis. In omphalocoele the cord inserts into the sac.
notes.E: A lateral defect favours gastroschisis. Omphalocoele is a midline defect at the umbilical ring.

ana-emb-es-95.why: A posterolateral diaphragmatic defect is a Bochdalek-type congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Abdominal viscera can enter the thorax through it and limit antenatal development of the adjacent lung.

notes.B: A hiatal hernia allows abdominal contents to pass through the oesophageal hiatus rather than through a posterolateral gap.
notes.C: Midgut malrotation changes the position and fixation of the bowel. It does not itself provide a passage through the diaphragm.
notes.D: Prolapse describes protrusion through an opening in general. The posterolateral diaphragmatic defect identifies a specific hernia at this site.
notes.E: A thoracic stomach describes an organ position. Other viscera may also pass through the same posterolateral diaphragmatic defect.

ana-emb-es-98.why: A double aortic arch is a vascular ring around the trachea and oesophagus. Any oesophageal narrowing results from external compression by the arteries rather than maldevelopment of the oesophageal wall.

notes.A: A tracheo-oesophageal fistula is a congenital communication between the developing foregut and respiratory passages.
notes.C: Oesophageal atresia is an interruption of the normal lumen that may leave a blind upper pouch, sometimes with a distal fistula.
notes.D: A congenital oesophageal web or septum can narrow the lumen by projecting into it from the wall.
notes.E: A congenitally short oesophagus can leave the gastro-oesophageal junction unusually high and is a developmental abnormality of the oesophagus.

ana-emb-es-101.why: Meckel’s diverticulum is a persistent ileal remnant of the vitelline duct. It is found in roughly two percent of people and is often asymptomatic.

notes.A: Oesophageal atresia is a congenital interruption of the oesophagus and is much less frequent than an incidental Meckel’s diverticulum.
notes.C: Omphalocoele is a relatively uncommon ventral wall defect containing herniated viscera within a sac at the cord insertion.
notes.D: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a recognised cause of gastric outlet obstruction but occurs less frequently than Meckel’s diverticulum.
notes.E: Congenital aganglionosis causes functional obstruction in the distal bowel and is less common than persistent ileal diverticulum.

ana-emb-es-103.why: The oesophageal muscularis externa is predominantly skeletal in its upper third and smooth in its lower third. The middle third contains a variable mixture of both.

notes.B: Mixed skeletal and smooth muscle is characteristic of the middle portion. The lower oesophageal wall is predominantly smooth muscle.
notes.C: This reverses the distribution. Striated skeletal muscle is proximal and smooth muscle predominates distally.
notes.D: The upper oesophageal muscularis is predominantly skeletal, continuing from the striated musculature of the pharyngeal region.
notes.E: The middle portion contains a mixture. The distal portion continues as smooth muscle towards the stomach.

ana-emb-es-104.why: The oesophagus develops entirely from dorsal foregut. It lengthens as thoracic organs descend, and its muscular wall changes from skeletal proximally to predominantly smooth muscle distally.

notes.B: The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm near vertebral level T10, contributing a normal site of constriction.
notes.C: The muscularis externa contains skeletal muscle proximally, smooth muscle distally and a mixture between these regions.
notes.D: A hiatal hernia can disrupt the normal anti-reflux barrier around the gastro-oesophageal junction and promote reflux.
notes.E: The dorsal oesophagus separates from the ventral respiratory tract during partitioning of the early foregut.

ana-emb-es-106.why: Incomplete recanalisation is the classical explanation for a membrane or narrowed lumen in the developing oesophagus. Other forms of congenital oesophageal stenosis have different wall abnormalities.

notes.A: Failure of foregut partitioning can leave a tracheo-oesophageal communication. A persistent intraluminal membrane reflects a different developmental process.
notes.C: Stomach rotation changes the orientation of the stomach and associated mesenteries. It does not govern reopening of the oesophageal lumen.
notes.D: Cloacal partition separates the lower anorectal and urogenital channels, far caudal to the developing oesophagus.
notes.E: Complete failure of separation would leave a common foregut passage. This differs from a narrowed lumen within a separate oesophagus.

ana-emb-es-107.why: Both an imperforate anus and distal aganglionosis can prevent the normal early passage of meconium. One obstructs the outlet structurally and the other obstructs it functionally.

notes.B: Forceful non-bilious projectile vomiting is characteristic of gastric outlet obstruction, especially infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
notes.C: Bilious vomiting can accompany intestinal obstruction, but delayed or absent meconium is the more characteristic shared initial clue here.
notes.D: Poor feeding can accompany neonatal illness generally. It does not localise an abnormality of the distal bowel or outlet.
notes.E: Explosive stool can follow rectal examination in Hirschsprung disease with a patent anus. It is not the typical shared presentation.

ana-emb-es-109.why: The ventral pancreatic bud rotates behind the duodenum and fuses with the dorsal bud. It forms the uncinate process and inferior portion of the head.

notes.A: The pancreatic neck derives mainly from the dorsal bud. It joins the head to the body in the mature gland.
notes.B: The body is derived from the dorsal pancreatic bud, which forms the bulk of the definitive gland.
notes.C: The tail develops from the dorsal bud and extends leftward in the direction of the spleen.
notes.E: Ventral derivatives are limited to the uncinate process and part of the head. The other listed regions are chiefly dorsal.

ana-emb-es-110.why: In the classical bifid-bud model, ventral pancreatic tissue passes on both sides of the duodenum and unites dorsally, leaving a ring that can narrow the lumen.

notes.A: The dorsal bud forms the bulk of the pancreas. In this model, tissue of ventral origin surrounds the duodenum.
notes.B: Abnormal ventral development is relevant, but a single unspecified rotation does not explain the classical two-limb mechanism.
notes.D: A duodenal obstruction can result from a pancreatic ring. Compression of the bud by a nearby duodenum does not create that ring.
notes.E: Failure of bud fusion or duct union can leave separate drainage pathways. It does not describe circumferential pancreatic tissue.

ana-emb-es-111.why: The three embryonic gut divisions have distinct axial arteries. The coeliac trunk supplies abdominal foregut, the superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut.

notes.A: The coeliac trunk supplies the abdominal foregut. Midgut and hindgut also contribute substantial parts of the abdominal gastrointestinal tract.
notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, including much of the small intestine and proximal colon. Foregut and hindgut have separate main arterial trunks.
notes.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut, including distal colon. It covers only one of the three embryonic territories.
notes.E: The three listed vascular trunks collectively supply the main foregut, midgut and hindgut territories within the abdomen.

ana-emb-es-114.why: Spaces within the lateral plate mesoderm unite to form the intraembryonic coelom. Its abdominal portion becomes the peritoneal cavity as the body cavities are partitioned.

notes.A: The extraembryonic coelom forms the chorionic cavity outside the embryo. It is distinct from the developing internal body cavities.
notes.C: Somatic mesoderm contributes to the parietal peritoneal lining. The cavity itself comes from the space between lateral plate layers.
notes.D: The yolk sac contributes endoderm to the developing gut tube. The peritoneal cavity lies outside the tube.
notes.E: The blastocyst cavity forms before implantation. The definitive peritoneal cavity develops later within lateral plate mesoderm.

ana-emb-es-115.why: The liver divides the ventral mesogastrium into the falciform ligament and lesser omentum. The hepatogastric ligament is the portion of the lesser omentum between liver and stomach.

notes.B: The splenorenal ligament is the dorsal mesogastric fold between the spleen and posterior abdominal wall near the left kidney.
notes.C: The gastrosplenic ligament is a dorsal mesogastric connection between the greater curvature of the stomach and the spleen.
notes.D: The dorsal mesogastrium expands into the greater omentum, including its part between the stomach and transverse colon.
notes.E: The transverse mesocolon begins as colonic dorsal mesentery and later fuses with the greater omentum derived from dorsal mesogastrium.

ana-emb-es-126.why: The embryonic foregut normally separates into a ventral respiratory tract and a dorsal oesophagus. Abnormal partitioning can leave a persistent opening between the two lumens.

notes.A: Abnormal septum development does explain a fistula. The ridge-fusion description is the corresponding classical account of septum formation.
notes.B: Improper ridge fusion is one classical description of defective foregut partitioning. The corresponding septal abnormality is also listed.
notes.C: Incomplete reopening of the oesophageal lumen can cause a web or narrowing. A fistula requires an abnormal connection to the respiratory tract.
notes.D: Excess epithelial growth can narrow or occlude a lumen. It does not by itself establish a separate opening into the trachea.

ana-emb-es-181.why: The embryonic midgut forms bowel from the distal duodenum through the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. The descending colon lies in the hindgut territory.

notes.A: The duodenum below the major papilla is midgut-derived and receives superior mesenteric branches through pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
notes.B: The jejunum is formed from the midgut loop. Its branches arise from the superior mesenteric arterial system.
notes.C: The ileum is a midgut derivative and develops in continuity with bowel adjoining the embryonic vitelline duct.
notes.D: The ascending colon develops from the caudal limb of the midgut loop and remains in the superior mesenteric territory.

ana-emb-es-182.why: The inferior mesenteric artery is the main axial vessel of the embryonic hindgut. Its left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal branches serve corresponding derivatives in the adult.

notes.A: The coeliac trunk principally supplies foregut derivatives such as the stomach and proximal duodenum.
notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut derivatives from distal duodenum through proximal transverse colon.
notes.D: Internal iliac branches can supply the lower rectum and pelvic structures. The inferior mesenteric artery is the main hindgut artery.
notes.E: The external iliac artery primarily continues into the lower limb as the femoral artery. It is not a gut axial vessel.

ana-emb-es-184.why: Gastroschisis exposes abdominal viscera through a full-thickness paraumbilical wall defect without a covering sac. Failed lateral body wall closure is one classical explanation for this morphology.

notes.A: Omphalocoele is centred at the umbilical ring and herniated viscera are ordinarily covered by a sac.
notes.C: Meckel’s diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline duct at the ileum. It is not an exposed abdominal wall defect.
notes.D: An umbilical hernia protrudes through the umbilical ring beneath the skin. A bare lateral defect is a different finding.
notes.E: Only gastroschisis matches exposed bowel through a lateral wall defect. The other conditions have different anatomy or coverings.

ana-emb-gpq-100.why: The primitive gut extends between the oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes. Gut endoderm forms the lining and many glandular cells, while splanchnic mesoderm provides smooth muscle and visceral coverings.

notes.A: The respiratory diverticulum marks the caudal level of the pharyngeal segment, where the ventral respiratory primordium forms.
notes.B: The foregut lies dorsal to the developing heart in the folded embryo. The heart tube is ventral to it.
notes.C: The early hindgut ends at the cloacal membrane, the temporary caudal boundary of the cloacal region.
notes.D: Gut-derived accessory glands such as the liver and pancreas have endodermal epithelial parenchyma and mesodermal supporting stroma.
notes.E: Splanchnic mesoderm provides gut smooth muscle and visceral serosa. Somatic mesoderm contributes to the parietal peritoneum.

ana-emb-gpq-148.why: Growth of the liver partitions the ventral mesogastrium into peritoneal folds around the liver and foregut. The greater omentum instead develops from the dorsal mesogastrium.

notes.A: The falciform ligament connects the developing liver to the anterior abdominal wall and carries the umbilical vein in its free edge.
notes.B: Peritoneal reflections from the liver to the diaphragm form the coronary ligaments around the bare area.
notes.C: The hepatoduodenal ligament is the thickened free edge of the lesser omentum, between the liver and proximal duodenum.
notes.D: The lesser omentum is the ventral fold from liver to stomach and proximal duodenum.
notes.E: The greater omentum extends from the greater gastric curvature and develops from elongation of the dorsal mesogastrium.

ana-emb-gpq-158.why: The ventral pancreatic bud forms part of the head and uncinate process. The dorsal bud forms most of the gland, and the two duct systems usually unite.

notes.A: The segment leading to the original dorsal opening can remain patent as the accessory duct at the minor papilla.
notes.B: The ventral duct forms the outlet segment of the main duct. The joined dorsal duct drains the body and tail.
notes.C: The uncinate process is a ventral bud derivative that passes behind the superior mesenteric vessels as the pancreas develops.
notes.D: The body and tail extend from the dorsal bud to form the elongated portion of the mature gland.
notes.E: The neck is chiefly dorsal in origin. The principal ventral derivatives are the uncinate process and inferior head.

ana-emb-sa-h-42.why: The metanephric mesenchyme develops within intermediate mesoderm and gives rise to nephrons. The adjacent ureteric bud induces these nephrons and separately forms their collecting system.

notes.A: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites and their derivatives. The nephrogenic cord forms lateral to the somites in intermediate mesoderm.
notes.B: Splanchnic mesoderm forms gut smooth muscle and visceral coverings. Renal nephrons arise from the metanephric mesenchyme.
notes.C: Somatic lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body wall structures and parietal serosa. It does not form the nephrogenic cord.
notes.D: Extraembryonic mesoderm supports structures such as chorion and connecting stalk. The nephron progenitors lie inside the embryo.

ana-emb-sa-h-43.why: The ureteric bud sprouts from the caudal mesonephric duct before it enters the cloaca. Its stalk forms the ureter and its branching tip forms collecting structures.

notes.A: The allantois connects to the developing bladder apex and contributes to the urachus. The ureteric bud sprouts more dorsally.
notes.C: The cloaca receives the mesonephric ducts. The bud emerges from a duct close to its cloacal entry.
notes.D: The common nephric duct is the segment caudal to the budding point. Its remodelling helps separate the ureteral and mesonephric openings.
notes.E: The primitive bladder receives the rearranged ureteral orifices later. The buds first grow from the paired mesonephric ducts.

ana-emb-sa-h-46.why: The common nephric duct is the short caudal mesonephric segment shared by the ureter and genital duct before their openings separate. Its remodelling helps position the ureter in the bladder wall.

notes.A: The paramesonephric duct contributes to female reproductive structures. It is distinct from the common segment linking the urinary ducts to the sinus.
notes.B: The ureteric bud forms the ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts. Its opening is repositioned during bladder development.
notes.C: The allantois connects at the bladder apex and becomes the urachus. The common duct remodels in the posterior bladder region.
notes.D: The vesical urogenital sinus gives rise to the developing bladder. Its wall receives the opening of the nephric duct system.

ana-emb-sa-h-49.why: A patent urachus retains a continuous channel from the bladder apex to the umbilicus. Raised bladder pressure from outlet obstruction can make urine discharge through it.

notes.A: A vitelline sinus is an umbilical remnant of the intestinal duct. Its secretion has no direct relationship to bladder outlet pressure.
notes.B: Mucus discharge can arise from an intestinal remnant. The combination of watery discharge and outlet obstruction favours a bladder connection.
notes.D: An umbilical hernia contains tissue protruding through the ring. Routine herniation does not create a channel from the bladder.
notes.E: Meckel’s diverticulum is usually blind-ending within the abdomen. Ulceration classically causes intestinal bleeding rather than urinary discharge.

ana-emb-es-80.why: Both major components of the definitive kidney arise in intermediate mesoderm. The metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons and the ureteric bud forms the ureter and collecting system.

notes.B: Lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body wall and visceral tissues. The nephrogenic cord is in intermediate mesoderm.
notes.C: Paraxial mesoderm produces somites, which contribute to vertebrae and skeletal muscle. The renal primordia arise lateral to them.
notes.D: Endoderm contributes much of the bladder epithelium through the urogenital sinus. The upper urinary tract is mesodermal.
notes.E: Ectoderm forms structures including epidermis and nervous tissue. Nephrons and ureters develop from the nephrogenic region of mesoderm.

ana-emb-es-82.why: As the kidneys ascend from the pelvis, each rotates medially around its longitudinal axis. This turns the hilum from an anterior orientation towards the midline.

notes.B: Rotation about a transverse axis would tilt the upper and lower poles. The typical change is medial orientation of the hilum.
notes.C: A sagittal axis runs from front to back. The kidney’s developmental rotation is around the line between its poles.
notes.D: The developing kidney turns around its own long axis, defined by the superior and inferior poles.
notes.E: An anteroposterior axis is horizontal in the anatomical position. The renal poles mark a roughly longitudinal axis.

ana-emb-es-83.why: Abnormal renal development can affect formation, fusion, ascent or tubule architecture. An accessory spleen instead reflects separate development of splenic tissue in the dorsal mesogastrium.

notes.A: A horseshoe kidney results from fusion, usually of the lower poles. The fused renal mass may have restricted ascent.
notes.B: A pelvic kidney remains low because the normal ascent of the metanephric kidney is incomplete.
notes.C: Renal agenesis results when a kidney fails to form, often because induction of metanephric tissue is disrupted.
notes.D: Polycystic kidney disease can present congenitally. Abnormal cyst formation occurs in renal tubular or collecting duct epithelium.

ana-emb-es-86.why: Developing renal lobes remain outlined by grooves at the fetal kidney surface. As surrounding cortical tissue grows after birth, the grooves often become less conspicuous.

notes.A: Distinct surface grooves are visible between lobes before the cortex smooths their outlines. Complete fusion would reduce visible lobulation.
notes.C: Cortical growth is associated with smoothing of the surface after birth. The fetal pattern reflects still-visible boundaries between lobes.
notes.D: Each lobe contains a medullary pyramid and related cortex. Normal fetal lobulation does not require degeneration of the medulla.
notes.E: Normal ureteric branching helps establish lobar territories. Visible fetal lobulation does not imply a branching anomaly.

ana-emb-es-141.why: The pronephros is the first, rudimentary nephric system and appears at the cranial end of the nephrogenic ridge. It regresses without serving as a functioning human kidney.

notes.A: The metanephros develops caudally in the pelvis and forms the permanent kidney following interaction with the ureteric bud.
notes.C: The temporary mesonephros forms caudal to the pronephros and develops more functional tubules during early embryonic life.
notes.D: The paramesonephric duct forms beside the mesonephros and contributes to reproductive structures rather than a cranial kidney system.
notes.E: The ureteric bud sprouts from the caudal mesonephric duct and induces the metanephros. It arises much farther caudally.

ana-emb-es-147.why: A horseshoe kidney usually forms when the lower poles of the two metanephric kidneys fuse. The connecting isthmus can limit their normal ascent into the abdomen.

notes.A: Unilateral agenesis means one kidney fails to form. It does not involve joining two renal poles.
notes.B: In bilateral agenesis, neither kidney develops. Fusion requires two developing renal masses.
notes.D: A pelvic kidney typically reflects failure of ascent. Fusion can restrict ascent but is not required for pelvic ectopia.
notes.E: Multicystic dysplastic kidney reflects abnormal renal differentiation with cysts and disorganised tissue. It is not defined by fusion.

ana-emb-es-149.why: The upper vesical portion of the primitive urogenital sinus expands to form most of the urinary bladder. Its apex is temporarily continuous with the allantois.

notes.A: The cloaca is the earlier common chamber. Its ventral urogenital subdivision supplies the immediate bladder primordium.
notes.C: The allantoic connection extends toward the umbilicus. The named bladder-forming region is the vesical part of the primitive urogenital sinus.
notes.D: The common nephric duct remodels near the posterior bladder and helps separate the duct openings. It does not produce most of the bladder.
notes.E: The ureteric bud forms the upper collecting tract. The bladder expands from the urogenital sinus.

ana-emb-sa-e-97.why: Mifepristone blocks progesterone receptor signalling. In pregnancy, this interferes with progesterone-dependent support of the decidua and increases uterine responsiveness to prostaglandins.

notes.A: Human chorionic gonadotrophin signals through the LH receptor to support early luteal function. It is not the direct target here.
notes.B: Human placental lactogen acts through lactogenic and related pathways. Mifepristone acts primarily at steroid receptors.
notes.C: Relaxin uses its own receptor and contributes to connective tissue and vascular changes. The drug does not directly block relaxin signalling.
notes.D: Mifepristone competes at progesterone receptors and blocks transcriptional responses that depend on progesterone.
notes.E: Oestrogen signals through distinct nuclear receptors. Mifepristone’s relevant direct target here is the progesterone receptor.

ana-emb-sa-h-50.why: The male mesonephric duct persists as much of the sperm-conducting tract. Seminiferous tubules instead develop from the testis cords within the gonadal primordium.

notes.A: The terminal mesonephric duct beyond the seminal vesicle outgrowth forms the ejaculatory duct.
notes.B: Each seminal vesicle forms as an outgrowth of the distal mesonephric duct and provides secretions to the genital tract.
notes.C: The duct of the epididymis develops from a coiled portion of the mesonephric duct. The efferent ductules come from mesonephric tubules.
notes.D: The mesonephric duct elongates into the ductus deferens, which carries sperm from the epididymis towards the ejaculatory duct.

ana-emb-sa-h-51.why: Differentiating Sertoli cells in the fetal testis secrete anti-Müllerian hormone. Its signalling induces regression of the Müllerian ducts, while androgen signalling supports separate male duct development.

notes.A: Primordial germ cells migrate to the genital ridge and form the germ line. Anti-Müllerian hormone comes from somatic Sertoli cells.
notes.C: Spermatogonia are germ-line cells in the testis cords and are precursors of sperm. They are not the source of the hormone.
notes.D: Testis cords contain developing Sertoli cells and germ cells. Sertoli cells are the specific secreting population within the cords.
notes.E: Surrounding mesenchyme participates in the duct’s response to the hormone. The fetal Sertoli cells provide the signal.

ana-emb-sa-h-52.why: Primordial germ cells migrate to the developing gonadal ridges. In a differentiating testis their descendants enter the germ cell lineage that gives rise to spermatogonia.

notes.A: Gonadal mesenchyme contributes supporting stroma and interstitial cells. Spermatogonia belong to the separate germ-cell lineage.
notes.B: Somatic testis cord cells include supporting Sertoli cells. The germ cells within the cords descend from migrating primordial germ cells.
notes.D: The mesonephric duct contributes to parts of the genital drainage tract. Its epithelial cells do not become spermatogonia.
notes.E: Coelomic epithelium forms part of the gonadal primordium. Germ-line precursors arrive by migration.

ana-emb-sa-h-53.why: The genital tubercle is the common early phallic primordium. In typical female development it gives rise to the clitoris, homologous to the male penis.

notes.A: The urogenital folds remain separate in typical female development and form the labia minora beside the vestibule.
notes.C: The mesonephric duct largely regresses in typical female development. It is not part of the external phallic primordium.
notes.D: Paramesonephric ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus and part of the vagina. The clitoris is external and tubercular in origin.
notes.E: The mesonephros is a temporary embryonic renal system. It does not give rise to the clitoris.

ana-emb-sa-h-54.why: The caudal paramesonephric ducts fuse to form the uterovaginal primordium, which gives rise to the uterus and cervix. The cranial portions remain separate as the uterine tubes.

notes.B: The oviducts are uterine tubes. They form from the cranial portions of the paramesonephric ducts that remain separate.
notes.C: The ovary develops within the gonadal ridge, where primordial germ cells join the supporting somatic cells.
notes.D: The labia minora form from the paired urogenital folds beside the developing vestibule.
notes.E: The labioscrotal swellings form the labia majora. They develop externally and are separate from the fused internal ducts.

ana-emb-sa-h-55.why: The ovary differentiates in the gonadal ridge after primordial germ cells arrive. These germ cells and somatic populations in the ridge participate in follicle formation.

notes.A: Genital swellings in the external primordia form the labia majora. The ovary develops internally in the gonadal ridge.
notes.B: The genital tubercle forms the clitoris in female development. It is part of the external genital primordium.
notes.C: The paired genital folds form the labia minora. They are external structures flanking the vestibule.
notes.E: The mesonephros is the transient embryonic renal system adjacent to the gonad. The ovarian primordium is the gonadal ridge.

ana-emb-sa-h-56.why: In the classical description, paired sinovaginal bulbs proliferate from the urogenital sinus where it meets the uterovaginal primordium. They form a solid vaginal plate that later canalises.

notes.B: The urogenital membrane forms a temporary covering over the early outlet and later ruptures. The epithelial proliferations arise from the sinus wall.
notes.C: The fused paramesonephric ducts form the uterovaginal primordium and contact the sinus. The sinovaginal bulbs are outgrowths at this junction.
notes.D: The genital tubercle gives rise to the clitoris in female development. The vaginal plate develops internally at the sinus.
notes.E: Genital folds flank the vestibule and give rise to the labia minora. They do not form the vaginal plate.

ana-emb-sa-h-58.why: The unfused cranial paramesonephric ducts give rise to the two uterine tubes. Their caudal portions instead unite to form the midline uterovaginal primordium.

notes.A: The genital folds remain separate as the labia minora. They are part of the external genital primordium.
notes.B: The genital ridge supplies the gonadal primordium. The uterine tubes form from the neighbouring paramesonephric ducts.
notes.C: The genital tubercle forms the clitoris in female development. The uterine tubes are internal duct derivatives.
notes.D: The mesonephric ducts largely regress in female development and may leave remnants, including Gartner duct tissue.

ana-emb-sa-h-59.why: The testis differentiates within the gonadal ridge. In typical 46,XY development, SRY-driven signalling promotes Sertoli cell differentiation and the organisation of testis cords.

notes.B: The mesonephros lies next to the gonad. Some mesonephric tubules form efferent ductules rather than the gonad itself.
notes.C: The genital tubercle forms the principal phallic primordium. It is separate from the developing testis.
notes.D: The genital folds contribute to the ventral penis and enclose much of the spongy urethra. They are external primordia.
notes.E: The labioscrotal swellings fuse to form the scrotum. The testis develops initially much higher at the gonadal ridge.

ana-emb-sa-h-60.why: The genital tubercle elongates to form the phallus under androgen signalling. In typical male development this forms most of the penis, with contributions from adjacent folds.

notes.B: The gonadal ridge differentiates into a testis. Hormones from the gonad influence development of the separate external genital primordia.
notes.C: The urethral folds join along the underside of the phallus, enclosing much of the urethra. The main phallic mass comes from the tubercle.
notes.D: The labioscrotal swellings fuse to form the scrotum. They do not form the main shaft of the phallus.
notes.E: The mesonephros is a transient renal structure. Its derivatives in the male tract do not form the external phallus.

ana-emb-sa-h-156-165.why: The gubernaculum guides testicular descent, with androgen signalling especially important during the inguinoscrotal phase. The processus vaginalis normally loses its connection to the peritoneal cavity.

notes.A: Androgen signalling is important in the later inguinoscrotal phase. INSL3 has a major role in the earlier transabdominal phase.
notes.B: The gubernaculum anchors and guides the testis during development. Abnormal gubernacular development can contribute to failed descent.
notes.C: The inguinal region develops before the testis traverses it. Descent uses and modifies a developing passage rather than initiating it.
notes.D: The distal processus vaginalis becomes the tunica vaginalis, which covers anterior and lateral surfaces without enclosing the posterior attachment.
notes.E: The internal spermatic fascia comes from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring as the testis passes through.
notes.F: The cremasteric fascia and muscle are derived chiefly from the internal oblique layer rather than the transversalis fascia.
notes.G: The external spermatic fascia is derived from the external oblique aponeurosis near the superficial inguinal ring.
notes.H: A patent processus vaginalis can transmit abdominal contents into the inguinal canal, producing an indirect hernia.

ana-emb-spm-4.why: Tight junctions between Sertoli cells separate the basal and adluminal compartments of seminiferous tubules. This limits exposure of developing germ cell antigens to the systemic immune environment.

notes.B: The basement membrane supports the seminiferous epithelium. The main barrier between basal and adluminal germ-cell compartments is junctional.
notes.C: Leydig cells lie in the interstitium and release testosterone. They are outside the Sertoli cell junctional barrier.
notes.D: Sertoli cell processes support and enclose developing germ cells locally. Tight junctions between neighbouring Sertoli cells provide the seal.
notes.E: Peritubular myoid cells surround the tubules and aid peristaltic movement. They do not separate basal from adluminal cells.

ana-emb-spm-6.why: Leydig cells in the testicular interstitium produce testosterone. Luteinising hormone stimulates their steroid synthesis, supporting spermatogenesis and androgen-dependent development.

notes.B: Sertoli cells support germ cells and respond to follicle-stimulating hormone. They are not the principal source of testosterone.
notes.C: Primary spermatocytes are germ cells undergoing meiosis. Testosterone is synthesised in adjacent interstitial Leydig cells.
notes.D: Myoid cells lie around seminiferous tubules and help propel luminal fluid. Their main role here is contractile.
notes.E: Spermatids are haploid germ cells that remodel into spermatozoa. They do not provide testicular androgen secretion.

ana-emb-spm-7.why: Adjacent Sertoli cells form tight junctions near the base of seminiferous tubules. These junctions create the blood–testis barrier and maintain a distinct environment for germ cells.

notes.B: Leydig cells are outside the tubules and produce testosterone. They do not form the epithelial junctional seal.
notes.C: Myoid cells form a contractile layer outside seminiferous epithelium. The barrier within the tubule is formed by Sertoli cells.
notes.D: Spermatogonia occupy the basal compartment and divide to supply germ cells. The junctional seal lies between supporting Sertoli cells.
notes.E: Fibroblasts produce extracellular matrix in supporting tissues. They do not form the tight junctions that divide the seminiferous epithelium.

ana-emb-spm-9.why: Pituitary luteinising hormone stimulates interstitial Leydig cells to produce testosterone at puberty. Its older name, interstitial cell-stimulating hormone, refers to that direct testicular action.

notes.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone acts primarily on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis. Leydig cell steroid production is stimulated directly by luteinising hormone.
notes.C: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone stimulates the pituitary to release gonadotrophins. It acts upstream of the direct Leydig cell signal.
notes.D: Inhibin from Sertoli cells provides negative feedback on pituitary follicle-stimulating hormone release. It does not stimulate Leydig cells.
notes.E: Prolactin is associated primarily with lactation and does not supply the main direct pubertal stimulus for testosterone production.

ana-emb-oog-4.why: The prepubertal ovarian reserve consists predominantly of primordial follicles. Each contains a primary oocyte arrested in meiotic prophase and surrounded by a single layer of flattened follicular cells.

notes.B: A unilaminar primary follicle has one layer of cuboidal follicular cells. This is an activated stage beyond the resting reserve.
notes.C: Multiple granulosa cell layers develop in growing primary follicles. They represent a smaller subset than the primordial pool.
notes.D: Antral follicles have a fluid-filled cavity and are more advanced. They do not make up most of the prepubertal reserve.
notes.E: A Graafian follicle is a large preovulatory follicle. Prepubertal ovaries contain mostly resting primordial follicles.

ana-emb-oog-14.why: Follicular atresia is degeneration of ovarian follicles that do not complete development. It occurs before birth and continues throughout reproductive life, gradually reducing the follicle reserve.

notes.B: Ovulation releases an oocyte from a selected mature follicle. It does not describe degeneration within the ovary.
notes.C: Luteinisation converts cells of an ovulated follicle into steroid-producing cells of the corpus luteum.
notes.D: Folliculogenesis refers to activation and growth of follicles. Atresia can interrupt that process at several stages.
notes.E: Menstruation is the shedding of uterine endometrium. It is separate from degeneration of ovarian follicles.

ana-emb-es-69.why: Fertilisation establishes the embryo’s chromosomal complement, including its sex chromosomes. Gonadal differentiation, hormone production and differentiation of ducts and external genitalia occur subsequently.

notes.A: External genitalia begin as common primordia. They differentiate later in response to local developmental and hormonal signalling.
notes.C: Both major duct systems are present in early embryos. Their subsequent development depends in part on gonadal hormone signals.
notes.D: The gonadal primordium initially has the potential to differentiate along different pathways, which become apparent weeks later.
notes.E: The developing gonads begin hormone production after they differentiate. These hormonal signals are downstream of the chromosomal complement.

ana-emb-es-70.why: When gonadectomy is chosen in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, its purpose is to reduce future testicular tumour risk. Risk varies with age, so timing is individualised.

notes.A: Undescended testes experience a warmer environment, but gonadectomy in this condition is considered principally for tumour risk reduction.
notes.B: Androgen receptor dysfunction explains the phenotype. Removing the gonads does not restore androgen receptor function.
notes.C: Torsion is possible for an undescended gonad, but it is not the usual rationale for elective removal in this syndrome.
notes.D: Removal does not improve fertility. The clinical consideration in this stem is long-term gonadal tumour risk.

ana-emb-es-74.why: The caudal Müllerian ducts fuse to form the uterovaginal primordium and generate the uterus and cervix. Failure of their formation or fusion can alter uterine development.

notes.B: The Wolffian ducts are mesonephric ducts. They form male internal genital duct structures when maintained by androgen signalling.
notes.C: The urogenital sinus contributes to the lower reproductive and urinary tract. The uterine primordium arises from the paired Müllerian ducts.
notes.D: Mesonephric ducts usually regress substantially in female development, whereas the paramesonephric ducts form the uterus.
notes.E: The urorectal septum separates developing anorectal and urogenital regions. It does not form the uterine wall.

ana-emb-es-75.why: A pathogenic SRY variant can prevent testis differentiation in a 46,XY embryo, producing complete gonadal dysgenesis. Other changes affecting the testis-determining pathway can produce the same phenotype.

notes.A: A Y chromosome is present in 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis. A defect in the developmental pathway can occur despite that chromosome.
notes.C: Müllerian structures can persist because dysgenetic gonads produce little anti-Müllerian hormone. Their persistence is a consequence.
notes.D: The genital tubercle forms external genital structures. Its development does not determine whether the gonadal ridge differentiates as a testis.
notes.E: Mesonephric ducts can regress when gonadal androgen production is insufficient. Their loss does not initiate failure of gonadal differentiation.

ana-emb-es-76.why: An imperforate hymen results when the hymenal membrane fails to open at the vaginal outlet. The canal above it can otherwise develop normally.

notes.B: Failure of Müllerian duct fusion can cause uterine duplication or a longitudinal vaginal septum, rather than an unperforated hymenal membrane.
notes.C: Abnormal fusion between developmental components can cause deeper partitions. An imperforate hymen is at the vaginal outlet.
notes.D: Cloacal malformations affect separation of the anorectal and urogenital tracts. An isolated imperforate hymen involves the outlet membrane.
notes.E: A persistent urogenital sinus can produce a shared lower tract opening. The specific defect here is failure of hymenal opening.

ana-emb-es-77.why: Dihydrotestosterone is formed from testosterone by 5-alpha reductase in target tissues. Its androgen receptor signalling promotes male differentiation of the genital tubercle and adjacent external folds.

notes.A: Oestrogen has roles in reproductive development but does not supply the principal androgen signal for penile differentiation.
notes.B: Anti-Müllerian hormone induces regression of the Müllerian ducts. It does not directly masculinise the genital tubercle.
notes.C: Testosterone supplies the substrate for dihydrotestosterone and directly maintains Wolffian ducts. Conversion produces the main external genital signal.
notes.D: Progesterone acts through its own receptor. It does not provide the main masculinising signal to the phallic primordium.

ana-emb-es-154.why: Prostatic glands develop as epithelial buds from the prostatic urethra, a derivative of the urogenital sinus. Surrounding mesenchyme provides the gland’s stromal and smooth muscle components.

notes.A: The cloaca is an earlier common chamber that gives rise to the urogenital sinus after partitioning. The sinus is the immediate source.
notes.C: The genital ridge forms the gonad. Prostatic gland buds instead grow from the adjacent urethral epithelium.
notes.D: The labioscrotal swellings form the scrotum in male development. They are external and do not form prostatic glands.
notes.E: The mesonephros is a transient kidney system. Prostatic epithelium arises from the urogenital sinus rather than from mesonephric tubules.

ana-emb-es-155.why: The uterus interrupts the female gubernaculum. Its segment from ovary to uterus forms the ovarian ligament, and the continuation toward the inguinal canal forms the uterine round ligament.

notes.A: The proper ovarian ligament is the segment of the gubernaculum between ovary and uterus. Its uterine continuation is also a derivative.
notes.B: The inguinal ligament is the rolled inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis. It is separate from the gubernaculum.
notes.C: The uterine round ligament is the segment continuing toward the inguinal canal. The segment above its uterine attachment also persists.
notes.D: The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum supporting the uterus and associated structures, with a different developmental origin.

ana-emb-es-156.why: Incomplete fusion of the paired Müllerian ducts can leave duplicated uterine and cervical structures and a longitudinal vaginal septum. Uterus didelphys is a recognised associated finding.

notes.B: Ovaries develop from the gonadal ridges, independently of Müllerian duct fusion. They can be present with uterine duplication.
notes.C: Imperforate hymen affects opening of the distal outlet membrane. It does not follow directly from duplication of the paired duct system.
notes.D: Hypospadias is abnormal positioning of the urethral opening, classically associated with incomplete male urethral development.
notes.E: Cloacal exstrophy involves a broader abdominal wall and pelvic developmental defect. It is not the characteristic association described here.

ana-emb-es-157.why: Local conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone provides the main androgen signal for typical male differentiation of external genital primordia, including the genital tubercle and urogenital folds.

notes.B: Oestrogen participates in other aspects of reproductive development. It is not the androgen receptor ligand directing external masculinisation.
notes.C: Anti-Müllerian hormone causes regression of internal Müllerian ducts, a separate process from differentiation of the external genitalia.
notes.D: Progesterone is important in reproductive physiology through progesterone receptors. The direct masculinising signal here acts through androgen receptors.
notes.E: Follicle-stimulating hormone acts on gonadal supporting cells. It is not the direct morphogenetic signal to the external genital primordia.

ana-emb-es-183.why: A persistent processus vaginalis leaves a channel between the peritoneal cavity and inguinal canal. Abdominal contents or fluid entering it can produce an enlarging groin swelling.

notes.A: Abnormal gubernacular development can impair testicular descent. An enlarging groin swelling fits a persistent channel that transmits fluid or viscera.
notes.C: An undescended testis can be palpable in the groin. A swelling that changes with herniation is more consistent with an open processus.
notes.D: Enlarged nodes can cause discrete groin lumps, but they do not provide a congenital channel from the abdominal cavity.
notes.E: In infants the typical indirect hernia follows the existing inguinal pathway through a patent processus rather than a primary muscle defect.

ana-emb-eg24-98-p16.why: Bilateral cryptorchidism puts both testes outside the cooler scrotal environment. Seminiferous epithelium and germ cells are particularly vulnerable, reducing sperm production and later fertility.

notes.B: Leydig endocrine function can be relatively preserved even when sperm production is impaired by the higher temperature.
notes.C: Ejaculation depends on separate ductal and neuromuscular pathways. In cryptorchidism the principal problem is production of mature sperm.
notes.D: Primary ciliary dyskinesia can impair sperm motility. It does not explain injury to the germinal epithelium of undescended testes.
notes.E: Dihydrotestosterone supports external genital development. Reduced spermatogenesis is the main mechanism asked for after bilateral non-descent.

ana-emb-eg24-99-p16.why: Ovulatory dysfunction is a common cause of female infertility. Without regular release of an oocyte, opportunities for spontaneous fertilisation decrease, even when the tubes and uterus are normal.

notes.B: Bilateral tubal obstruction prevents sperm and oocyte meeting. It is an important cause, but ovulatory dysfunction is more common overall.
notes.C: Coital factors can reduce opportunities for fertilisation. The common reproductive mechanism listed here is disruption of oocyte release.
notes.D: Endometrial receptivity matters for implantation, but isolated timing of the endometrial cycle is not the leading established cause listed.
notes.E: Endometriosis can affect fertility through pelvic inflammation or altered anatomy. Ovulatory problems are reported more commonly overall.

ana-emb-eg24-146-p24.why: The blood–testis barrier forms at junctions between neighbouring Sertoli cells. Their seals separate basal spermatogonia from germ cells undergoing later stages of development in the adluminal compartment.

notes.A: Spermatogonia are germ cells in the basal compartment. The seal is formed by adjacent somatic supporting cells.
notes.B: Sertoli cells closely support spermatocytes, but the continuous junctional barrier lies between neighbouring Sertoli cells.
notes.D: Each tubule contains its own junctional barrier. A boundary between two tubules is outside the seminiferous epithelium.
notes.E: Leydig cells and peritubular myoid cells lie outside the seminiferous epithelium. The tight junctions are within that epithelium.

ana-emb-eg24-149-p25.why: Leydig cells secrete testosterone, while the seminiferous epithelium produces the male germ cells and Sertoli cells contribute luminal fluid. The pituitary supplies the testis-regulating gonadotrophins.

notes.A: Androgen secretion and germ-cell production are both testicular functions. Sertoli cells also provide fluid within the seminiferous tubules.
notes.B: The testis does produce testosterone and male germ cells. Luteinising hormone is released by anterior pituitary gonadotrophs.
notes.C: Testicular fluid is produced locally, but both gonadotrophins originate in the anterior pituitary and act on the testis.
notes.E: The testis supplies germ cells and testicular fluid. Follicle-stimulating hormone comes from the anterior pituitary.

ana-emb-sa-e-115.why: Neural crest cells migrate from the closing neural tube and generate multiple peripheral lineages, including sensory neurons, Schwann cells, pigment cells and adrenal chromaffin cells.

notes.A: Migrating melanoblasts derived from the neural crest populate tissues such as skin and differentiate into melanocytes.
notes.B: Schwann cells develop from neural crest derivatives and form supporting and myelinating glia around peripheral axons.
notes.C: Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells belong to the neural crest lineage and secrete catecholamines into the circulation.
notes.D: Embryonic dermatomes form from somites in paraxial mesoderm. They contribute to dermis rather than a neural crest lineage.
notes.E: Neural crest cells form the sensory neurons and supporting glia of the dorsal root ganglia.

ana-emb-sa-h-7.why: Microglia arise mainly from early yolk-sac macrophage precursors that colonise the developing central nervous system. Ependymal cells, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes instead derive from neural tube progenitors.

notes.B: Ependymal cells arise from neuroepithelial or radial glial progenitors and form the lining of the ventricles and spinal central canal.
notes.C: Astrocytes differentiate from central neuroectodermal progenitors and provide support within neural tissue.
notes.D: Oligodendrocytes arise from progenitors within the developing central nervous system and form central myelin.
notes.E: Microglia provide a clear exception because their normal developmental origin is the embryonic myeloid lineage.

ana-emb-sa-h-61-64.why: Congenital obstruction at a ventricular connection can prevent normal cerebrospinal fluid drainage. Fluid accumulates upstream and enlarges the affected ventricles, producing obstructive hydrocephalus.

notes.A: Aqueductal obstruction prevents fluid passing from the third to the fourth ventricle and enlarges the upstream ventricles.
notes.B: The interventricular foramina allow drainage from each lateral ventricle. Obstruction can cause enlargement of the affected lateral ventricle.
notes.C: The median and lateral fourth ventricular apertures allow fluid to reach the subarachnoid space. Their obstruction raises upstream volume.
notes.D: Choroid plexus contributes to fluid production. Its failure to develop is not a blockage at a ventricular outlet.

ana-emb-sa-h-65-68.why: A meningocoele is a cerebrospinal fluid-containing protrusion of meninges without neural tissue in the sac. Myelocoele leaves the abnormal neural placode exposed at the surface.

notes.A: Meninges protrude through the vertebral defect and enclose cerebrospinal fluid. A membrane or skin can cover the swelling.
notes.B: A simple meningocoele contains no spinal cord or nerve roots in the sac. Associated anomalies are possible but do not define it.
notes.C: In an open myelocoele, the unfused neural placode can appear as an exposed raw plate without a raised meningeal sac.
notes.D: Myelocoele involves abnormal exposed neural tissue and can produce neurological deficits. The cord and nerves are not normally developed there.

ana-emb-sa-h-69-73.why: The hindbrain subdivisions form the pons and medulla at different levels. Farther rostrally, the mesencephalic cavity persists as the aqueduct and forebrain cavities become the lateral and third ventricles.

notes.A: The medulla derives from the myelencephalon. The metencephalon forms the pons and cerebellum.
notes.B: The pons forms ventrally within the metencephalon, while the cerebellar primordium develops dorsally.
notes.C: The third ventricle is primarily diencephalic. Classical accounts also include a small midline telencephalic contribution at its rostral end.
notes.D: The mesencephalic lumen persists as the cerebral aqueduct linking the third and fourth ventricles.
notes.E: The hippocampal formation develops in the medial telencephalic wall as part of the cerebral pallium.

ana-emb-es-136.why: The adrenal cortex develops from mesodermal coelomic epithelial cells. The adrenal medulla is developmentally distinct and is populated by chromaffin cells of neural crest lineage.

notes.A: Spinal sensory ganglion neurons are neural crest derivatives and lie in the dorsal root ganglia.
notes.B: Schwann cells are neural crest derivatives that associate with axons in peripheral nerves.
notes.C: Neural crest-derived melanoblasts migrate and differentiate into melanocytes in tissues such as the epidermis.
notes.D: Chromaffin cells are adrenal medullary derivatives of the neural crest lineage and release catecholamines.

ana-emb-sa-h-15.why: The thyroid primordium originates in the midline pharyngeal floor near the future foramen caecum. Failure of its normal descent can leave thyroid tissue at the tongue base.

notes.B: Altered mucosal covering would not account for the thyroid remaining at its early position. The gland normally descends into the neck.
notes.C: The hypobranchial eminence forms part of the posterior tongue. The thyroid begins as a distinct median endodermal primordium.
notes.D: Location at the foramen caecum is explained by persistence along the normal thyroid pathway, without requiring abnormal lingual covering.
notes.E: The midline location is a recognised site of thyroid ectopia because it corresponds to the primordium’s site of origin.

ana-emb-sa-h-20.why: The stomodeum is the early ectodermal depression of the mouth. Its deep boundary is the buccopharyngeal membrane, which breaks down to open into the foregut.

notes.A: The pericardial region lies caudal to the developing mouth. It does not separate the oral depression from the foregut.
notes.B: The frontonasal process lies above the stomodeum and contributes to the forehead and nose.
notes.C: Lateral nasal prominences form later around the nasal pits. They are not the membrane at the bottom of the oral depression.
notes.D: The developing forebrain lies superior to the stomodeum. The deep oral boundary is a separate endoderm–ectoderm interface.

ana-emb-sa-h-21.why: Mesenchyme covering the ventral aspect of the forebrain expands into the frontonasal prominence. This median facial primordium forms the upper border of the developing mouth.

notes.B: The buccopharyngeal membrane is an epithelial boundary where ectoderm and endoderm meet, rather than a mesenchymal prominence.
notes.C: The maxillary processes are paired outgrowths of the first pharyngeal arch and border the stomodeum laterally.
notes.D: The mandibular processes are paired first-arch structures and form the lower border of the developing mouth.
notes.E: The stomodeum is a depression between facial prominences. It is not a mesenchymal outgrowth from the forebrain region.

ana-emb-sa-h-23.why: Each nasal placode invaginates into a nasal pit. The mesenchyme bordering its medial and lateral edges grows into the paired medial and lateral nasal prominences.

notes.A: The frontonasal process carries the placodes, but the pits provide the immediate landmarks around which the nasal prominences appear.
notes.C: The lens placode forms where the optic vesicle contacts surface ectoderm. It is separate from the nasal placode and pit.
notes.D: The philtrum forms after the paired medial nasal prominences merge. It is a later component of the upper lip.
notes.E: The upper lip forms after fusion of facial prominences, including the medial nasal and maxillary components.

ana-emb-sa-h-25.why: The upper frontal region of the frontonasal prominence forms the forehead. The lower part carries the nasal placodes and contributes to development of the nose.

notes.B: The central lower part of the frontonasal prominence contributes to the nasal region. The forehead is derived more superiorly.
notes.C: The medial nasal prominences merge to form midline nasal structures and the intermaxillary segment, including the philtral component.
notes.D: The lateral nasal prominences contribute to the alae of the nose. They do not extend into the forehead.
notes.E: The philtrum is the midline contour of the upper lip and forms from the merged medial nasal prominences.

ana-emb-sa-h-28.why: The paired maxillary prominences expand laterally around the developing mouth and contribute to the cheeks. They also form much of the upper jaw and lateral upper lip.

notes.A: The upper frontonasal prominence forms the forehead and lies above the areas developing into the cheeks.
notes.B: The central frontonasal region forms part of the nose. The cheeks develop from a first-arch prominence on each side.
notes.D: Lateral nasal prominences contribute to the nasal alae. The adjacent cheek mesenchyme is mainly maxillary in origin.
notes.E: The lateral nasal–maxillary boundary is associated with the nasolacrimal groove. The cheeks arise principally from maxillary prominences.

ana-emb-sa-h-29.why: The primary palate forms anterior to the incisive foramen. The fused secondary palatal shelves contribute most of the remaining hard palate and continue posteriorly into the soft palate.

notes.A: The primary palate contributes the small premaxillary region anterior to the incisive foramen. Most of the hard palate is posterior to it.
notes.B: The secondary palate supplies most of the hard palate, but the primary palate contributes the anterior premaxillary part.
notes.D: Posterior regions of the palatal shelves contribute to the soft palate. Most hard palate forms from more anterior ossifying tissue.
notes.E: Fusion of posterior shelf tissue helps form the soft palate. The complete hard palate includes the primary palate as well.

ana-emb-sa-h-30.why: The nasal septum grows inferiorly from the midline frontonasal tissue. It divides the nasal cavity and joins the developing palatal structures along the midline.

notes.B: The philtrum is an external midline feature of the upper lip. It is separate from the internal nasal partition.
notes.C: Lateral palatal shelves arise from the maxillary prominences. They meet the septum during fusion but do not form it.
notes.D: The septum has a frontonasal origin. Neither the philtrum nor the lateral palatal shelves is its source.
notes.E: The frontonasal prominence supplies the midline tissue that extends down to become the nasal septum.

ana-emb-sa-h-31.why: Peripheral cells of the neural crest-derived dental papilla differentiate into odontoblasts and deposit dentine. The central region of the papilla becomes the dental pulp.

notes.A: The dental lamina forms tooth germs from oral epithelium. It does not provide the mesenchymal cells that produce dentine.
notes.B: Outer dental epithelium is the outer boundary of the enamel organ. Odontoblasts arise in the adjacent dental papilla.
notes.C: Inner dental epithelium gives rise to ameloblasts, the cells that produce enamel facing the developing dentine.
notes.D: The stellate reticulum is an epithelial support network of the enamel organ. It does not differentiate into odontoblasts.

ana-emb-sa-h-32.why: Inner dental epithelial cells differentiate into ameloblasts at the enamel organ’s interface with the dental papilla. The ameloblasts deposit enamel on the developing dentine surface.

notes.A: The dental lamina is the epithelial precursor of the tooth germ. The immediate source of ameloblasts is the inner enamel epithelium.
notes.B: Outer dental epithelium forms the outer surface of the enamel organ. Ameloblasts differentiate on its inner surface.
notes.D: The stellate reticulum supports the enamel organ and helps maintain its shape. It is not the secretory ameloblast layer.
notes.E: The dental papilla supplies odontoblasts for dentine and cells of the pulp. Enamel is made by an epithelial lineage.
