ana-emb-sa-h-33.why: Most tongue muscles arise from migrating occipital myotome cells and retain hypoglossal innervation. Palatoglossus is a pharyngeal arch muscle and has vagal innervation.

notes.A: The lateral lingual swellings form much of the mucosa of the anterior tongue. Their surface contribution is separate from muscle origin.
notes.B: The tuberculum impar is a median first-arch swelling. It is largely overgrown by the paired lateral swellings.
notes.D: The copula is an early midline swelling that is overgrown during posterior tongue development. It does not supply the main muscle lineage.
notes.E: The hypobranchial eminence contributes to mucosal regions of the posterior tongue. Most tongue muscle comes from migrating myotomes.

ana-emb-sa-h-34.why: The posterior third of the tongue develops mainly from the third-arch part of the hypobranchial eminence. The more caudal fourth-arch region contributes near the epiglottis.

notes.A: The paired lateral lingual swellings are first-arch structures that form most of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
notes.B: The tuberculum impar lies between the lateral lingual swellings and is overgrown as the anterior tongue forms.
notes.C: Occipital myotomes supply most tongue muscles. The surface mucosa of the posterior region comes from pharyngeal arch swellings.
notes.D: The second-arch copula is overgrown by the hypobranchial eminence, which forms most of the posterior mucosa.

ana-emb-sa-h-118-125.why: A typical bilateral cleft upper lip reflects failure of union on both sides between the maxillary prominences and the medial nasal-derived intermaxillary segment that forms the philtrum.

notes.A: The frontonasal prominence normally gives rise to the medial nasal structures. Bilateral clefts can occur with these structures present.
notes.B: On the right, failure of union between the maxillary prominence and the future philtral segment leaves a cleft beside the midline.
notes.C: The same failed junction on the left leaves the other cleft, separating the central segment from the lateral lip.
notes.D: The lateral nasal–maxillary junction is associated with the nasolacrimal groove, which is not the usual cleft-lip site.
notes.E: On the left, failure at the lateral nasal junction would involve a more lateral facial boundary near the nasolacrimal tract.
notes.F: The right maxillary prominence must join medial nasal-derived tissue to complete the right side of the upper lip.
notes.G: Failure of the corresponding left maxillary–medial nasal union produces the left-sided defect in a bilateral cleft.
notes.H: Failure of the two medial nasal prominences to join affects the midline. A typical bilateral cleft instead flanks the central segment.

ana-emb-es-2.why: Pharyngeal clefts are the surface ectodermal grooves between neighbouring arches. Internal endodermal pockets are the pharyngeal pouches, which meet the clefts at thin intervening membranes.

notes.B: A pharyngeal membrane lies where a pouch and cleft approach one another. The external indentation itself is the cleft.
notes.C: Pouches are endoderm-lined pockets projecting from the inside of the embryonic pharynx between arches.
notes.D: The cervical sinus forms when the second arch grows over more caudal clefts. It is not the general term for the external grooves.
notes.E: Stenosis describes narrowing of a lumen. The normal surface boundaries between pharyngeal arches are grooves.

ana-emb-es-3.why: The first pharyngeal cleft is the ectodermal groove between the first and second arches. Classically it contributes the external acoustic meatus toward the tympanic membrane.

notes.A: The auditory tube is derived from the endodermal tubotympanic recess of the first pouch, on the internal side.
notes.B: The auricle forms from hillocks around the first cleft, with contributions from the first and second arches.
notes.D: The malleus is a derivative of a skeletal condensation of the first pharyngeal arch rather than from the surface groove.
notes.E: The tympanic membrane has several tissue layers, including outer ectoderm at the first-cleft boundary. The cleft’s canal derivative is the meatus.

ana-emb-es-5.why: Hemifacial microsomia is a presentation within the craniofacial microsomia spectrum, typically involving unilateral underdevelopment of first- and second-arch structures. Goldenhar describes overlapping oculoauriculovertebral features.

notes.B: Mandibulofacial dysostosis describes several syndromes, often with bilateral zygomatic and mandibular hypoplasia. It is distinct from typical hemifacial microsomia.
notes.C: Microtia is underdevelopment of the external ear. It can be a feature of this spectrum but names only one finding.
notes.D: Robin sequence involves a small mandible, posterior tongue displacement and airway obstruction. It is a different clinical pattern.
notes.E: Treacher Collins syndrome is a mandibulofacial dysostosis with frequently bilateral findings. The synonyms here point to the craniofacial microsomia spectrum.

ana-emb-es-6.why: The stomodeum is the primitive ectoderm-lined oral depression between developing facial prominences. It opens into the foregut after the buccopharyngeal membrane breaks down.

notes.A: The buccopharyngeal membrane temporarily separates the oral depression from the foregut and breaks down during development.
notes.B: Oropharyngeal membrane is another term for the transient partition at the depth of the oral depression.
notes.C: The stomodeal membrane is the temporary boundary at the base. The stomodeum itself is the primitive oral cavity.
notes.E: The proctodeum is the ectodermal depression at the caudal end of the gut and contributes to the lower anal canal.

ana-emb-es-7.why: The mandibular prominences arise from the first pharyngeal arches and supply the mesenchyme of the lower jaw. Excess lower-jaw growth corresponds to that developmental territory.

notes.B: The maxillary prominences form much of the upper jaw, cheeks and portions of the upper lip and palate.
notes.C: Medial nasal prominences contribute midline nasal and intermaxillary structures, including the philtral region of the upper lip.
notes.D: Lateral nasal prominences form the alae of the nose. They are separate from the lower jaw primordia.
notes.E: The frontonasal prominence forms the forehead and much of the nose. The lower jaw arises from paired first-arch prominences.

ana-emb-es-12.why: The sixth pharyngeal arch is associated with the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus. It supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles that differentiate within this arch territory.

notes.A: The cranial accessory designation is historically associated with fibres joining the vagus, but it does not name the sixth arch branch.
notes.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve is associated with the third arch and supplies its stylopharyngeus muscle.
notes.C: Pharyngeal branches of the vagus help innervate the pharynx. The named sixth arch supply is the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
notes.E: The superior laryngeal branch is associated with the fourth arch, including innervation of the cricothyroid muscle.

ana-emb-es-15.why: Stylopharyngeus is the characteristic muscle of the third pharyngeal arch. It retains glossopharyngeal innervation and elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing.

notes.A: Cricothyroid arises in the fourth arch territory and receives the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
notes.B: Levator veli palatini belongs to the fourth arch group in the classical account and is supplied through the pharyngeal plexus.
notes.C: The posterior digastric belly is a second-arch muscle and receives its motor supply from the facial nerve.
notes.D: Thyrohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle supplied by cervical fibres travelling with the hypoglossal nerve. It is not a third-arch muscle.

ana-emb-es-16.why: The ventral third pharyngeal pouch forms thymic epithelium, and its dorsal portion forms the inferior parathyroids. Their descent explains why the third-pouch glands end up lower.

notes.B: Palatine tonsillar epithelium comes from the second pharyngeal pouch. Surrounding lymphoid cells populate it later.
notes.C: The pharyngeal tonsil develops in the roof of the nasopharynx. It is not paired with the thymus as a third-pouch derivative.
notes.D: The superior parathyroids are derived from the fourth pharyngeal pouches and migrate a shorter distance than the inferior glands.
notes.E: The ultimobranchial body is associated with the caudal pharyngeal pouch complex and joins the thyroid rather than the thymus.

ana-emb-es-17.why: Olfactory or nasal placodes are paired ectodermal thickenings on the lower frontonasal prominence. Their invagination establishes nasal pits and helps define adjacent nasal prominences.

notes.A: The buccopharyngeal membrane is a transient partition between the oral depression and foregut. It does not carry the nasal placodes.
notes.C: The philtrum develops later from merged medial nasal tissue and lies in the upper lip.
notes.D: Maxillary prominences flank the mouth and contribute to the upper jaw and lateral upper lip. The olfactory placodes lie higher.
notes.E: The medial nasal prominences form beside nasal pits after the olfactory placodes begin to invaginate.

ana-emb-es-18.why: Microstomia is an abnormally small oral opening. Congenital cases may reflect excessive union of the maxillary and mandibular facial components at the oral commissure.

notes.A: Hemifacial microsomia describes asymmetric underdevelopment of craniofacial structures, often including the mandible and ear.
notes.B: Möbius syndrome typically involves congenital facial weakness and impaired ocular abduction. It does not name a small oral opening.
notes.C: Mandibulofacial dysostosis describes a developmental pattern of facial skeletal abnormalities rather than the specific size of the mouth opening.
notes.D: Micrognathia describes a small jaw. The question identifies a small oral aperture at the commissure.

ana-emb-es-20.why: The mandibular prominences of the first pharyngeal arch form the lower margin of the stomodeum. The maxillary prominences border it laterally, and the frontonasal prominence lies above.

notes.B: The maxillary process is also from the first arch, but it forms the side boundary of the primitive mouth.
notes.C: The lateral nasal prominence lies beside a nasal pit, superior to the first-arch lower margin of the stomodeum.
notes.D: The stomodeum is the primitive mouth depression. Its inferior margin is formed by the paired mandibular prominences.
notes.E: The buccopharyngeal membrane closes the deep boundary of the stomodeum, separating it from the underlying foregut.

ana-emb-es-47.why: The oropharyngeal membrane, also called the buccopharyngeal membrane, initially separates the stomodeum from the foregut. It ruptures around the fourth week as the mouth opens.

notes.A: The cloacal membrane is at the caudal end of the embryonic gut, far from the oral depression.
notes.B: The laryngotracheal groove forms in ventral foregut and initiates respiratory development. It is not the oral boundary.
notes.C: The oesophagus forms farther caudally from dorsal foregut. Its opening does not name the membrane at the mouth.
notes.E: The proctodeum is an ectodermal depression at the caudal outlet. It contributes to the lower anal canal.

ana-emb-es-51.why: The broad frontonasal process above the stomodeum supplies the early upper face. Its frontal region forms the forehead and its lower components contribute to the nose.

notes.A: Medial nasal processes arise around the nasal pits within the frontonasal region and form more local midline structures.
notes.B: Lateral nasal processes form at the outer edges of the nasal pits and contribute mainly to the alae.
notes.C: Maxillary processes lie on either side of the primitive mouth and contribute to the upper jaw and cheeks.
notes.D: Mandibular processes form the lower facial region, including the lower jaw and lower lip.

ana-emb-es-52.why: A transverse facial cleft causing macrostomia occurs when maxillary and mandibular prominences fail to unite normally at the lateral oral commissure. This widens the mouth opening.

notes.A: Failure at the medial nasal–maxillary junction produces a typical upper-lip cleft beside the philtrum.
notes.B: The lateral nasal–maxillary boundary follows the nasolacrimal groove. A defect there can produce an oblique facial cleft.
notes.D: Failure of the medial nasal prominences to unite can affect midline nasal or upper-lip structures, away from the oral commissure.
notes.E: A cleft due to failed union between mandibular prominences lies in the midline of the lower jaw or lip.

ana-emb-es-53.why: Short palpebral fissures are one of three characteristic facial findings used in assessment for fetal alcohol syndrome. The others are a smooth philtrum and thin upper vermilion.

notes.B: The characteristic lip finding is a thin upper vermilion border. Lip thickness is assessed with an appropriate reference guide.
notes.C: Nasal bridge shape can vary and is not a defining facial criterion. Short horizontal eyelid openings are a characteristic finding.
notes.D: A large mandible is not a characteristic feature. Some affected children have a small mandible or midface hypoplasia.
notes.E: Nasal width is not one of the characteristic diagnostic facial measurements. The palpebral fissures, philtrum and upper vermilion are assessed.

ana-emb-es-54.why: Lateral nasal prominences form the outer borders of the early nasal pits and develop into the alae. The merged medial prominences contribute to the central nasal region.

notes.A: The medial processes contribute to central nasal structures and the intermaxillary segment. The alae are formed laterally.
notes.C: The maxillary processes form the cheeks and much of the upper jaw. They meet lateral nasal tissue near the nasolacrimal groove.
notes.D: Mandibular processes form the lower jaw and lower lip. They are not the immediate source of the nasal alae.
notes.E: The frontonasal process is the parent region. The lateral nasal prominences are its direct local derivatives forming the alae.

ana-emb-es-55.why: The upper lip and primary palate depend on union of maxillary tissue with the medial nasal-derived intermaxillary segment. Clefts extending into secondary palate also involve the palatal shelves.

notes.B: Failure at the lateral nasal–maxillary junction is associated with an oblique facial cleft near the nasolacrimal groove.
notes.C: The maxillary–mandibular junction forms the lateral oral commissure. Its failure leads to a transverse facial cleft or macrostomia.
notes.D: The frontonasal process contributes to the medial nasal prominences. The relevant junction is more specifically between medial nasal and maxillary tissue.
notes.E: Failure of the medial nasal prominences to unite affects midline facial development. A typical upper-lip cleft lies to one side of the midline.

ana-emb-es-56.why: Most tongue muscles arise from myotomes of the occipital somites. Their precursors migrate into the tongue and retain hypoglossal innervation, with palatoglossus a pharyngeal arch exception.

notes.B: Pharyngeal arch regions give rise to tongue mucosa and the arch muscle palatoglossus. Most intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles come from occipital myotomes.
notes.C: Neural crest cells contribute craniofacial connective tissues and other supporting structures. Tongue myofibres are mainly myotomal mesoderm.
notes.D: Endoderm contributes much of the posterior tongue’s epithelial lining. It does not supply the migrating muscle precursors.
notes.E: Ectoderm can contribute surface epithelium in the oral region. The tongue skeletal muscles do not arise from this lining.

ana-emb-es-57.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue. It also carries taste from circumvallate papillae near the boundary.

notes.A: The facial nerve carries taste from most of the anterior two-thirds through the chorda tympani.
notes.C: The vagus carries taste from the epiglottic region, farther caudally than the usual posterior lingual territory.
notes.D: The hypoglossal nerve supplies most tongue muscles. It does not carry taste from lingual taste buds.
notes.E: The lingual branch of the mandibular trigeminal nerve carries general sensation from the anterior tongue. Taste fibres travelling with it belong to the facial nerve.

ana-emb-es-59.why: Each third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to thymic epithelial tissue ventrally and an inferior parathyroid primordium dorsally. Both migrate caudally before separating.

notes.A: Thymic epithelium does develop from the ventral third pouch. Its dorsal companion is also a derivative.
notes.B: Inferior parathyroids develop from the dorsal third pouch, which also gives rise to the thymus ventrally.
notes.C: Palatine tonsillar epithelium arises from the second pouch. It is not part of the third-pouch pair.
notes.E: The inferior parathyroids are correctly included. Tonsillar tissue is the misplaced second-pouch derivative in this combination.

ana-emb-es-60.why: The third pharyngeal arch contributes the greater horns and lower part of the hyoid body. The lesser horns arise from second-arch skeletal tissue.

notes.A: The stylohyoid ligament develops along the second-arch cartilage lineage. It connects the styloid process to the hyoid.
notes.C: The lesser horn is a second-arch derivative, along with the upper portion of the hyoid body in the classical account.
notes.D: Thyroid cartilage is part of the laryngeal skeleton, which develops from more caudal arch territories than the hyoid greater horns.
notes.E: Cricoid cartilage also belongs to the laryngeal skeleton and forms from caudal arch mesenchyme.

ana-emb-es-61.why: Tensor tympani is a first-arch muscle supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Stapedius and the other listed second-arch muscles receive facial nerve supply.

notes.A: Stapedius is a second-arch muscle in the middle ear and receives a branch of the facial nerve.
notes.B: Stylohyoid is derived from the second arch and is innervated by the facial nerve.
notes.C: The posterior belly of digastric has second-arch origin and facial innervation. The anterior belly belongs to the first arch.
notes.E: Muscles of facial expression are derived from second-arch myoblasts and retain facial nerve innervation after migration.

ana-emb-es-63.why: Endoderm of the second pharyngeal pouch forms the epithelium and crypts of the palatine tonsil. Lymphoid cells subsequently populate the connective tissue around those crypts.

notes.A: The first pouch forms the tubotympanic recess, which contributes to the auditory tube and middle ear.
notes.C: The third pouch gives rise to thymic epithelium and the inferior parathyroids. The palatine tonsil has a different pouch origin.
notes.D: The first arch forms structures such as the jaw primordia and muscles of mastication. Tonsillar epithelium is pouch endoderm.
notes.E: The second arch contributes facial expression muscles and hyoid-related skeletal structures. Its adjacent pouch has a distinct endodermal lineage.

ana-emb-es-64.why: The second arch skeletal primordium, Reichert’s cartilage, gives rise to structures including the stylohyoid ligament, lesser horn of the hyoid and much of the stapes.

notes.A: The stapes superstructure is classically a second-arch derivative. The footplate has a more complex origin near the otic capsule.
notes.B: The stylohyoid ligament is associated with Reichert’s cartilage and runs between the styloid process and hyoid.
notes.C: The lesser horn belongs to the second-arch contribution to the hyoid. The greater horn is attributed to the third arch.
notes.D: The malleus is a first-arch ossicle associated with the proximal region of Meckel’s cartilage.
notes.E: The incus is also a first-arch ossicle, connecting the malleus to the stapes in the middle ear.

ana-emb-es-65.why: The paired first-arch lateral lingual swellings normally unite at the midline. Incomplete merging can leave a bifid tongue with a cleft at its tip.

notes.A: Agnathia refers to absence of a jaw, usually the mandible. It does not describe separation of the anterior tongue.
notes.B: Ankyloglossia limits movement of the tongue because of its lingual frenulum. It does not create a bifid tip.
notes.D: Macroglossia is enlargement of the tongue, which can occur even when the lingual swellings fuse normally.
notes.E: Microglossia is an abnormally small tongue. Incomplete fusion characteristically produces a midline division instead.

ana-emb-es-66.why: The paired lateral lingual swellings arise in the first pharyngeal arch. They enlarge and merge over the median tuberculum impar to form most of the anterior tongue mucosa.

notes.B: The second arch contributes the transient copula, which is overgrown during development of the posterior tongue.
notes.C: The third arch supplies much of the posterior third mucosa through the hypobranchial eminence.
notes.D: The fourth arch contributes to the most caudal tongue region near the epiglottis, farther back than the paired lateral swellings.
notes.E: The conventionally numbered fifth arch is rudimentary or absent in usual descriptions and supplies no anterior tongue swelling.

ana-emb-es-67.why: The foramen caecum marks the midline site where the thyroid primordium starts in the developing tongue. The thyroid normally descends through the neck from that region.

notes.A: The parathyroids arise from paired pharyngeal pouches, with inferior glands from the third and superior glands from the fourth.
notes.B: Palatine tonsillar epithelium is derived from the second pharyngeal pouch, at a lateral pharyngeal site.
notes.D: The thymic epithelium arises from the ventral third pouch and migrates toward the anterior mediastinum.
notes.E: The major salivary glands bud from oral epithelium at their own sites. The midline foramen is a landmark of the thyroid pathway.

ana-emb-es-68.why: Thyroid parafollicular cells develop in the ultimobranchial body, a derivative of the caudal pharyngeal pouch complex. It joins the developing thyroid and supplies its calcitonin-secreting cells.

notes.A: The median thyroid diverticulum is the main primordium for follicular epithelium. The parafollicular cells reach it through the separate ultimobranchial body.
notes.B: The lateral lingual swellings form anterior tongue mucosa, far from the caudal pouch that contributes parafollicular cells.
notes.C: The tuberculum impar is a first-arch midline lingual swelling. It is separate from the migrating pouch-derived tissue.
notes.E: Vallate papillae are lingual taste-associated structures. They do not provide a lineage for thyroid endocrine cells.

ana-emb-es-158.why: Inferior parathyroids arise from the dorsal third pharyngeal pouches and descend with the thymus. Superior parathyroids arise from the fourth pouches and usually migrate a shorter distance.

notes.A: The first pouch forms the tubotympanic recess, and the second gives rise to palatine tonsillar epithelium.
notes.B: The third pouch provides the inferior glands. The superior glands come from the fourth pouch rather than the second.
notes.D: The fourth pouch contributes only the superior set. The inferior set migrates from the third pouch.
notes.E: The first pouch forms the tubotympanic recess and does not give rise to the parathyroids.

ana-emb-gpq-101.why: Pharyngeal endoderm contributes to posterior tongue lining, the thyroid primordia and thymic epithelium. The developing mouth also contains ectodermal epithelium, which produces enamel and classically the parotid buds.

notes.A: Ameloblasts differentiate from oral ectoderm-derived dental epithelium. They secrete enamel rather than pharyngeal endoderm forming it.
notes.B: The posterior tongue mucosa is associated with pharyngeal arch endoderm. Much of the anterior oral lining has a different origin.
notes.C: The thyroid follicular primordium arises in the midline pharyngeal floor and descends into the neck.
notes.D: The parotid bud is classically described as an outgrowth of oral epithelium on the ectodermal side.
notes.E: Thymic epithelial cells arise from the ventral third pouch. Developing lymphocytes later populate that epithelial framework.

ana-emb-gpq-102.why: First-arch mesenchyme contributes jaw-associated skeletal structures and several muscles supplied by mandibular trigeminal fibres. This includes the incus, mylohyoid and tensor veli palatini.

notes.A: The incus is a first-arch auditory ossicle, along with the malleus, associated with Meckel’s cartilage.
notes.B: The sphenomandibular ligament persists along the first-arch mandibular cartilage pathway between sphenoid and mandible.
notes.C: The posterior digastric belly belongs to the second arch and receives facial nerve supply. The anterior belly is first-arch derived.
notes.D: Mylohyoid is a first-arch muscle. Its nerve comes from the inferior alveolar branch of the mandibular trigeminal division.
notes.E: Tensor veli palatini is innervated by the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve, consistent with its first-arch origin.

ana-emb-gpq-103.why: The third arch contributes the greater horn and lower body of the hyoid. Its characteristic muscle is stylopharyngeus, which is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

notes.A: Stylohyoid belongs to the second-arch muscle group and is supplied by the facial nerve.
notes.B: Stylopharyngeus is the characteristic third-arch muscle and receives branches from the glossopharyngeal nerve.
notes.C: The greater horn is a third-arch skeletal derivative. The lesser horn is classically attributed to the second arch.
notes.D: The styloid process is associated with Reichert’s cartilage of the second arch rather than the third arch.
notes.E: Palatopharyngeus develops in the more caudal pharyngeal muscle group and receives vagal fibres through the pharyngeal plexus.

ana-emb-gpq-104.why: The first pouch extends as the tubotympanic recess. Its lumen contributes the auditory tube and middle-ear space, and its endoderm forms the inner layer of the tympanic membrane.

notes.A: The expanded distal recess contributes to the tympanic cavity surrounding the developing ossicles.
notes.B: The mastoid antrum forms as an extension of the developing middle-ear space posteriorly.
notes.C: The tubotympanic recess is the elongating first-pouch outgrowth that establishes the tube and cavity.
notes.D: Endoderm from the first pouch forms the inner mucosal layer. The outer epithelial layer comes from surface ectoderm.
notes.E: The narrower proximal part of the recess persists as the auditory tube connecting the nasopharynx and tympanic cavity.

ana-emb-gpq-105.why: The second arch overgrows the more caudal surface clefts and encloses a transient cervical sinus. Persistence of ectodermal remnants can produce a lateral cervical cyst.

notes.A: The cervical sinus is the temporary recess created by overgrowth of the second pharyngeal arch over caudal clefts.
notes.B: A branchial cyst may develop when tissue lining the cervical sinus persists instead of regressing.
notes.C: Thymic epithelium arises from endoderm of the third pouch. The cervical sinus is a surface ectodermal feature.
notes.D: The superior parathyroid develops from the fourth pouch, an internal endodermal recess.
notes.E: The ultimobranchial body is derived from the caudal pouch complex and later joins the developing thyroid.

ana-emb-gpq-106.why: The medial nasal prominences merge and contribute the philtrum, while maxillary tissue forms the lateral upper lip. Mandibular prominences unite below the mouth to form the lower lip.

notes.A: Merged medial nasal prominences form the intermaxillary segment, whose superficial labial component is the philtrum.
notes.B: The nasolacrimal groove separates the maxillary prominence from the lateral nasal prominence and contributes the drainage pathway.
notes.C: The lateral nasal prominences form the nasal alae. The upper lip is derived from medial nasal and maxillary tissue.
notes.D: The paired mandibular prominences unite in the midline and contribute the lower lip.
notes.E: By around ten weeks the principal facial features have formed. Growth and remodelling continue thereafter.

ana-emb-es-23.why: The apical ectodermal ridge is a thickened band at the distal tip of the limb bud. Its fibroblast growth factors maintain proliferation of underlying mesenchyme and support outgrowth.

notes.B: Somatic lateral plate mesoderm supplies the limb bud mesenchyme. The surface ridge is an ectodermal signalling structure.
notes.C: Somitic mesoderm sends muscle precursors into the limb. It is not the distal surface tissue maintaining outgrowth.
notes.D: The posterior zone of polarising activity patterns the thumb-to-little-finger axis through Sonic hedgehog signalling.
notes.E: The underlying mesenchyme proliferates in response to signals. The named surface source of those signals is the ectodermal ridge.

ana-emb-es-28.why: Once a limb bud has been initiated, growth along its proximal–distal axis depends on reciprocal signalling with the apical ectodermal ridge. Ridge-derived fibroblast growth factors sustain distal outgrowth.

notes.B: The zone of polarising activity lies posteriorly and patterns the anterior–posterior sequence of digits.
notes.C: The somatic mesodermal core produces several limb tissues and interacts with the ridge. The distal ectodermal ridge supplies the specific outgrowth signals.
notes.D: Ventral ectoderm contributes to dorsal–ventral patterning and helps position the ridge at the interface with dorsal ectoderm.
notes.E: Dorsal ectoderm provides positional signals for dorsal limb identity. The distal ridge maintains proximal–distal outgrowth.

ana-emb-es-30.why: Syndactyly is persistent union of adjacent digits. Failure of normal regression of interdigital tissue can leave soft-tissue webbing, and some forms also include fusion of bones.

notes.B: Ectrodactyly involves absence of one or more digits or rays, often with a central cleft in the hand or foot.
notes.C: Polydactyly causes one or more extra digits. It is distinct from continued attachment between adjacent digits.
notes.D: Brachydactyly describes abnormally short digits, usually because of shortened bones in the hand or foot.
notes.E: Symbrachydactyly features short or absent digits and can also include webbing. The stated isolated separation defect is syndactyly.

ana-emb-es-31.why: Amelia is complete absence of one or more limbs. When some limb components are present and other parts are missing, terminology depends on the pattern of partial absence.

notes.B: Hemimelia denotes a partial limb deficiency. Complete absence of the entire limb is a different category.
notes.C: Meromelia describes partial absence of a limb, with at least some structures such as a proximal or distal segment present.
notes.D: Phocomelia is a severe limb reduction in which hands or feet can remain close to the trunk despite shortened or absent long bones.
notes.E: Sirenomelia is fusion and malformation of the lower limbs, often with associated internal abnormalities.

ana-emb-es-32.why: Upper limb buds become visible first in the fourth week. Lower limb buds appear shortly afterward, typically about two days later in the standard developmental sequence.

notes.B: The visible lower buds follow within the same general fourth-week window, so a full week is longer than the usual interval.
notes.C: By two weeks after upper limb budding, the lower limbs are already in further stages of growth and patterning.
notes.D: Four weeks later the limbs are much more advanced. The initial upper and lower buds emerge days apart.
notes.E: The upper buds become visible first. Lower buds follow shortly afterward, with timing varying somewhat by embryonic stage.

ana-emb-sa-a-8.why: Embryology explains how normal anatomy, fetal membranes and congenital abnormalities develop. Hormonal deficiencies as a general subject are addressed more directly through physiology and clinical endocrinology.

notes.A: Embryonic development helps explain the adult positions of the testes and the courses of the recurrent laryngeal nerves.
notes.B: Study of fetal membranes and placental relationships provides a foundation for obstetrics and perinatal anatomy.
notes.C: Congenital abnormalities often reflect deviations from normal development, so embryology helps explain their anatomical patterns.
notes.E: Embryology connects microscopic tissue differentiation with gross anatomy, providing context across the morphological disciplines.

ana-emb-sa-b-11.why: The spermatogonial stem-cell pool is in the type A population near the seminiferous tubule basement membrane. It self-renews and generates progenitors that enter the differentiating pathway.

notes.A: Spermatids are haploid products of meiosis. They differentiate into spermatozoa without renewing the basal germ-cell pool.
notes.C: Type B spermatogonia are committed differentiating cells that produce primary spermatocytes. They follow the renewing type A population.
notes.D: Primary spermatocytes enter the first meiotic division. They are downstream of mitotically active spermatogonia.
notes.E: Secondary spermatocytes form after meiosis I and enter meiosis II. They have already left the mitotic stem-cell stage.

ana-emb-sa-b-15.why: The mid-cycle luteinising hormone surge directly triggers follicular rupture and oocyte release. It also promotes resumption of oocyte meiosis and luteinisation of the remaining follicular cells.

notes.A: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone controls pituitary gonadotrophin secretion. The pituitary luteinising hormone surge acts directly on the ovary.
notes.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone supports follicle growth and granulosa cell function. It is not the principal direct trigger for rupture.
notes.D: Sustained preovulatory oestradiol causes positive feedback leading to the luteinising hormone surge. Its role is upstream of follicular rupture.
notes.E: Progesterone rises after luteinisation and acts on the endometrium. It is not the main trigger for ovulation.

ana-emb-sa-b-16.why: Pituitary luteinising hormone supports steroid production by the corpus luteum during the menstrual cycle. In early pregnancy, human chorionic gonadotrophin provides the signal that rescues it from regression.

notes.A: Follicle-stimulating hormone mainly supports the growing follicle. Luteal steroid production depends more directly on luteinising hormone.
notes.C: Human chorionic gonadotrophin is produced after implantation and maintains the corpus luteum of early pregnancy rather than the ordinary cycle.
notes.D: Human chorionic somatomammotrophin is placental lactogen. It has metabolic and mammary effects and does not sustain the menstrual corpus luteum.
notes.E: Placental thyroid-stimulating activity is distinct from luteotrophic signalling. Pituitary luteinising hormone is the relevant support in the non-pregnant cycle.

ana-emb-sa-c-52-71.why: Human oocytes enter meiosis before birth and arrest in prophase I. The ovulated secondary oocyte has 23 duplicated chromosomes and normally finishes meiosis II only after fertilisation.

notes.A: Mitotic proliferation of oogonia normally occurs prenatally. The postnatal oocyte pool consists of cells already committed to meiosis.
notes.B: Oocytes in neonatal primordial follicles have entered meiosis I and are arrested in its prophase.
notes.C: The finite ovarian reserve declines largely through atresia. Reproductive ovulatory cycles generally cease at menopause.
notes.D: A primary oocyte is diploid with 46 chromosomes. After DNA replication each chromosome comprises two sister chromatids.
notes.E: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosome pairs. A secondary oocyte has 23 chromosomes, each still having two sister chromatids.
notes.F: The secondary oocyte is haploid in chromosome sets with twice the DNA content of a mature haploid gamete, not fourfold.
notes.G: Meiosis II separates the remaining sister chromatids and allows extrusion of the second polar body after activation.
notes.H: Polar bodies produced by normal oocyte meiosis are haploid. Their chromosomes are duplicated after the first division and unduplicated after the second.
notes.I: The maternal pronucleus normally provides an X chromosome. The fertilising sperm normally provides either X or Y.
notes.J: A typical secondary oocyte contains one X chromosome and no Y chromosome. X–Y variation usually comes from sperm.
notes.K: The ovulated oocyte is generally fertilisable for roughly a day. Fourteen days is closer to the length of a typical luteal phase.

ana-emb-sa-c-63-81.why: Diploid spermatogonia proliferate by mitosis and give rise to primary spermatocytes. Meiosis produces haploid spermatids, which remodel into spermatozoa without any further division.

notes.A: Spermatids have 23 chromosomes after meiosis II, which separates the sister chromatids of secondary spermatocytes.
notes.B: A typical human spermatozoon is haploid and carries 23 chromosomes, including one sex chromosome.
notes.C: A primary spermatocyte has 46 chromosomes. After premeiotic DNA replication these consist of paired sister chromatids.
notes.D: Secondary spermatocytes have 23 chromosomes after homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I.
notes.E: Type A spermatogonia are diploid and have 46 chromosomes before they give rise to differentiating descendants.
notes.F: Type B spermatogonia also have 46 chromosomes and still belong to the diploid mitotic compartment.
notes.G: The type A population undergoes mitosis, supporting both renewal and production of differentiating germ-cell progenitors.
notes.H: Type B spermatogonia divide mitotically. Their primary spermatocyte descendants undergo the first meiotic division.
notes.I: Primary spermatocytes are committed to meiosis I, which separates homologues rather than sister chromatids.
notes.J: Secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis II, separating sister chromatids and producing haploid spermatids.
notes.K: Spermatids have completed meiosis. They remodel their nuclei, cytoplasm and flagellar apparatus during spermiogenesis.
notes.L: A spermatozoon is the mature product of spermatogenesis and does not restart that developmental programme.
notes.M: Spermiogenesis is the differentiation of a spermatid into a spermatozoon without a further cell division.
notes.N: The type A population includes renewing cells and differentiating progenitors, whose descendants give rise to type B spermatogonia.
notes.O: Type B spermatogonia undergo their final mitotic divisions before their descendants differentiate into primary spermatocytes.
notes.P: Meiosis I of a primary spermatocyte first produces secondary spermatocytes. Spermatids are the next meiotic products.
notes.Q: Secondary spermatocytes give rise to spermatids through meiosis II. Spermatids do not divide to reverse that sequence.
notes.R: Epididymal sperm undergo functional maturation and storage, while mitotic proliferation is restricted to earlier spermatogonia in the testis.

ana-emb-spm-2.why: A secondary spermatocyte forms after meiosis I and has one set of duplicated chromosomes. It completes meiosis II to separate sister chromatids and form spermatids.

notes.A: The primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis I, which separates homologous chromosomes and forms secondary spermatocytes.
notes.C: A spermatid is the product of meiosis II and differentiates without another division during spermiogenesis.
notes.D: Type B spermatogonia undergo mitotic division and are the precursors of primary spermatocytes.
notes.E: A spermatozoon is a terminally differentiated haploid cell. It is produced by spermiogenesis rather than another meiotic division.

ana-emb-spm-3.why: Type B spermatogonia are committed diploid germ cells. After their final mitotic divisions, the descendants differentiate into primary spermatocytes and enter the first meiotic division.

notes.B: Secondary spermatocytes are formed only after primary spermatocytes complete meiosis I and separate their homologous chromosomes.
notes.C: Spermatids are postmeiotic cells formed when secondary spermatocytes complete meiosis II.
notes.D: Type B spermatogonia are the precursor population named in the question. Their differentiating descendants enter the primary spermatocyte stage.
notes.E: A spermatozoon forms by remodelling a spermatid after both meiotic divisions, well downstream of spermatogonial mitosis.

ana-emb-spm-5.why: Spermiogenesis transforms a haploid spermatid into a spermatozoon without division. The nucleus condenses, an acrosome and flagellum develop, and much of the excess cytoplasm is lost.

notes.B: Secondary spermatocytes complete meiosis II to produce spermatids. Those spermatids are the cells that subsequently remodel.
notes.C: Primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis I and produce secondary spermatocytes. The sperm-shaped stage comes later.
notes.D: A spermatozoon is the product of spermiogenesis. It undergoes later functional maturation in the epididymis.
notes.E: Type A spermatogonia belong to the early mitotic population and provide progenitors for the meiotic lineage.

ana-emb-oog-1.why: Meiotic cytokinesis in oogenesis is unequal. A small polar body receives chromosomes and little cytoplasm, while the larger daughter retains the cytoplasm needed to support early development.

notes.B: The secondary oocyte receives most of the cytoplasm during meiosis I, leaving little for the first polar body.
notes.C: The primary oocyte is the large precursor that enters meiosis I. It is not the small meiotic daughter.
notes.D: The ootid is the large functional product after meiosis II. The second polar body receives much less cytoplasm.
notes.E: Oogonia are prenatal mitotic germ cells. They precede primary oocytes and are not products of meiotic cytokinesis.

ana-emb-oog-2.why: By ovulation, the primary oocyte has usually completed meiosis I and expelled its first polar body. The ovary releases the secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II.

notes.B: A primary oocyte retains homologous chromosome pairs and precedes completion of meiosis I. The ovulated cell has passed this stage.
notes.C: The ootid forms when meiosis II is completed, normally after sperm entry activates the ovulated secondary oocyte.
notes.D: The first polar body can remain under the zona pellucida, but the functional cell released is the secondary oocyte.
notes.E: Oogonia proliferate during fetal ovarian development and give rise to primary oocytes long before ovulation begins.

ana-emb-oog-3.why: Follicle-stimulating hormone acts on granulosa cells and supports maturation of growing ovarian follicles. Later in the cycle a luteinising hormone surge directly triggers ovulation.

notes.B: Luteinising hormone acts on theca cells and triggers ovulation in a surge. Follicle-stimulating hormone directly supports granulosa growth.
notes.C: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone acts on the pituitary to release follicle-stimulating and luteinising hormones, rather than acting directly on follicles.
notes.D: Oestrogen is produced by growing follicles and provides feedback to the reproductive axis. It is not the pituitary follicle-stimulating signal.
notes.E: Progesterone derives predominantly from the luteal phase corpus luteum. Its major cyclic role is supporting secretory endometrium.

ana-emb-oog-5.why: During the transition from primordial to primary follicle, the flattened follicular cells become cuboidal. A single cuboidal layer identifies the unilaminar stage before granulosa cells proliferate further.

notes.A: Primordial follicles have a single layer of flattened follicular cells. Cuboidal cells indicate activation into a primary follicle.
notes.C: A multilaminar primary follicle has several granulosa cell layers rather than a single layer.
notes.D: An antral follicle has a fluid-filled space within the granulosa cell layers, a later developmental feature.
notes.E: A Graafian follicle is a large preovulatory antral follicle. Its cavity and granulosa organisation go beyond the single cuboidal layer.

ana-emb-oog-6.why: Growing follicles produce oestrogen through cooperation between two cell types. Theca cells supply androgen substrate, and granulosa-cell aromatase converts it to oestradiol under follicle-stimulating hormone influence.

notes.B: Progesterone becomes the predominant luteal steroid after ovulation. The characteristic cooperative product of the growing follicle is oestradiol.
notes.C: Luteinising hormone comes from the anterior pituitary and stimulates theca androgen synthesis. It is a signal to the follicle.
notes.D: Follicle-stimulating hormone is a pituitary gonadotrophin. It promotes granulosa aromatase activity rather than being made by follicular cells.
notes.E: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone is produced by the hypothalamus and controls pituitary gonadotrophin release upstream of ovarian steroid synthesis.

ana-emb-oog-8.why: An antrum begins when small fluid pockets within the granulosa layer coalesce. In the terminology used here this transition identifies the secondary, or antral, follicle.

notes.A: A primordial follicle has a primary oocyte and one surrounding layer of flattened cells. Its small structure has no antrum.
notes.B: The unilaminar primary stage has one cuboidal follicular cell layer before a fluid cavity develops.
notes.C: A multilaminar primary follicle is preantral in this classification, even though it has several granulosa layers.
notes.E: The Graafian follicle has a large, established antrum. The cavity first appears earlier during antral development.

ana-emb-oog-10.why: The antrum occupies most of a mature Graafian follicle. The oocyte is displaced toward the periphery and remains attached to the granulosa wall through the cumulus oophorus.

notes.A: A primordial follicle has flattened supporting cells around the oocyte and no fluid-filled antrum.
notes.B: A unilaminar primary follicle has one layer of cuboidal cells and has not yet developed a fluid cavity.
notes.C: The multilaminar primary stage adds several granulosa layers, but it is still preantral in this classification.
notes.D: Early antral follicles have a cavity that is still developing. A large dominant cavity characterises the mature stage.

ana-emb-oog-11.why: After follicular rupture, remaining granulosa and theca cells luteinise and form the corpus luteum. This temporary endocrine gland secretes progesterone to support the secretory endometrium.

notes.B: The corpus albicans is the fibrous scar left after the corpus luteum regresses. It is not the active postovulatory gland.
notes.C: An atretic follicle degenerates without completing the normal ovulatory sequence. It does not form a functioning postovulatory gland.
notes.D: A Graafian follicle is the mature preovulatory follicle. Luteinisation after rupture produces the temporary gland.
notes.E: Theca externa forms a supporting connective tissue layer around a follicle. The luteal steroid cells are derived mainly from granulosa and theca interna.

ana-emb-oog-12.why: The corpus luteum produces predominantly progesterone after ovulation, along with oestrogen. Its progesterone converts the oestrogen-primed endometrium into a secretory lining suitable for implantation.

notes.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone originates in anterior pituitary gonadotrophs and supports follicular development earlier in the cycle.
notes.C: Luteinising hormone is a pituitary signal that promotes luteinisation and supports luteal activity. The corpus luteum responds to it.
notes.D: Human chorionic gonadotrophin from trophoblast maintains luteal function in early pregnancy. It is not a major corpus luteum product.
notes.E: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone comes from hypothalamic neurons and regulates pituitary secretion upstream of the ovary.

ana-emb-oog-13.why: The preovulatory luteinising hormone surge promotes completion of meiosis I. This produces a secondary oocyte and a first polar body, with the secondary oocyte arresting again in meiosis II.

notes.B: Meiosis II reaches metaphase before ovulation but normally completes only after the secondary oocyte is activated by fertilisation.
notes.C: Oogonial mitosis belongs to fetal ovarian development. The growing preovulatory cell is already a meiotic oocyte.
notes.D: Fertilisation normally occurs in the uterine tube after ovulation releases the secondary oocyte from the follicle.
notes.E: Zona pellucida deposition starts in growing follicles well before the preovulatory resumption of meiosis.

ana-emb-oog-15.why: A primary oocyte initiates meiosis during fetal life and pauses at diplotene of prophase I. This arrest can last for years until the follicle approaches ovulation.

notes.B: Metaphase I occurs after the primary oocyte resumes its first meiotic division near ovulation.
notes.C: Metaphase II is the later arrest of the ovulated secondary oocyte. The fetal arrest occurs during the first meiotic division.
notes.D: The long arrest is in prophase I. The secondary oocyte progresses into the second division only after meiosis I finishes.
notes.E: The oocyte has already entered meiosis by the time prolonged arrest begins. It does not remain in premeiotic interphase.

ana-emb-oog-16.why: The zona pellucida is an extracellular glycoprotein coat deposited around the growing oocyte. It lies between the oocyte surface and surrounding follicular cells and later participates in fertilisation.

notes.B: The corona radiata consists of living granulosa cells that lie just outside the zona pellucida.
notes.C: Theca interna is the steroidogenic layer outside the granulosa compartment. It is not the coat immediately surrounding the oocyte.
notes.D: A follicular basement membrane lies outside the granulosa layer, separating it from the theca rather than from the oocyte.
notes.E: The cumulus oophorus is a cluster of granulosa cells surrounding and attaching the oocyte to the follicle wall.

ana-emb-oog-17.why: The corona radiata is the innermost layer of cumulus granulosa cells immediately external to the zona pellucida. These cells remain associated with the oocyte at ovulation.

notes.B: Theca interna lies outside the follicular basement membrane and supplies steroid precursors to granulosa cells.
notes.C: Theca externa is the outer supporting layer of the follicle. It is not carried away with the ovulated oocyte.
notes.D: Membrana granulosa denotes the granulosa lining of the follicle wall. The corona radiata is the specialised layer immediately surrounding the oocyte.
notes.E: The zona pellucida is an acellular glycoprotein coat. The surrounding cellular layer is made of granulosa cells.

ana-emb-es-34.why: Asthenozoospermia is reduced sperm motility. It can occur despite a normal sperm concentration and morphology because movement is a separate semen parameter.

notes.A: Aspermia means no semen is emitted. The stem describes an ejaculate that contains spermatozoa.
notes.B: Azoospermia means no sperm are identified in the ejaculate. Here sperm are present at a normal count.
notes.D: Oligozoospermia refers to a low sperm concentration. The abnormality described concerns the proportion of motile sperm.
notes.E: Teratozoospermia refers to an increased proportion of morphologically abnormal sperm. The given morphology is normal.

ana-emb-eg24-36-p6.why: Fertilisation normally activates the secondary oocyte to complete meiosis II and extrude the second polar body. The retained maternal chromosomes then form the female pronucleus.

notes.B: An oogonium is an earlier mitotically dividing germ-cell precursor found during fetal ovarian development.
notes.C: A primary oocyte is present before completion of meiosis I and has the original diploid chromosome complement.
notes.D: The secondary oocyte is the product of meiosis I and is the cell that undergoes meiosis II.
notes.E: The retained haploid maternal chromosomes form the female pronucleus, which is explicitly included among the choices.

ana-emb-eg24-63-p11.why: Homologous chromosomes pair and then separate during meiosis I of the primary spermatocyte. Each daughter secondary spermatocyte receives one homolog from each pair, with sister chromatids still joined.

notes.A: Pale type A spermatogonia belong to the mitotic germ-cell population. They do not segregate homologous chromosome pairs in meiosis.
notes.B: Dark type A spermatogonia are undifferentiated germ cells. They precede the cells that undergo meiotic chromosome segregation.
notes.C: Type B spermatogonia are differentiating mitotic cells whose descendants enter meiosis as primary spermatocytes.
notes.E: A secondary spermatocyte already contains one chromosome from each homologous pair. It separates sister chromatids during meiosis II.

ana-emb-eg24-64-p11.why: In spermatogenesis the secondary spermatocyte enters meiosis II with duplicated chromosomes. Sister chromatids separate during that division to produce spermatids with unduplicated haploid chromosome sets.

notes.A: Pale type A spermatogonia can separate sister chromatids during ordinary mitosis. The context here is the meiotic stage of spermatogenesis.
notes.B: Dark type A cells are undifferentiated spermatogonia and are distinct from the cells performing the second meiotic division.
notes.C: Type B spermatogonia are mitotic precursors. Their descendants enter meiosis as primary spermatocytes.
notes.D: The primary spermatocyte separates homologous chromosomes in meiosis I. Sister chromatids stay joined until meiosis II.

ana-emb-eg24-80-p13.why: Spermatogenesis is sensitive to increased testicular temperature, ionising radiation, cytotoxic treatment and testicular inflammation. Migraine itself is not a recognised direct injury to the germinal epithelium.

notes.A: Normal core temperature is higher than the scrotal temperature favourable to spermatogenesis. Prolonged exposure to that heat can impair germ cells.
notes.B: Ionising radiation can damage dividing spermatogonia and related germ cells, reducing later sperm production.
notes.C: Antimitotic drugs can injure actively dividing germ cells and lower the output of the seminiferous epithelium.
notes.D: Mumps orchitis causes testicular inflammation and can impair spermatogenesis, especially when both testes are affected.

ana-emb-eg24-90-p15.why: The oocyte supplies virtually all the zygote’s cytoplasm and most organelles, including the inherited mitochondrial population. The sperm provides paternal chromosomes and a small contribution of cellular components.

notes.B: The sperm contributes paternal DNA and factors involved in activation and early organisation. It supplies little cytoplasmic volume.
notes.C: Gametes contribute comparable haploid chromosome sets, but their cytoplasmic volumes are very different.
notes.D: The male pronucleus contains the paternal chromosome set. It is a nuclear structure within the oocyte-derived cytoplasm.
notes.E: The large oocyte supplies the cytoplasmic mass that sustains the early embryo before its own gene expression increases.

ana-emb-eg24-106-p18.why: Developing oocytes enter meiosis in fetal life and pause in the diplotene stage of prophase I. Selected oocytes resume that division in mature follicles after puberty.

notes.A: Anaphase I is when homologous chromosomes separate, after the prolonged prophase arrest has already been lifted.
notes.B: Metaphase II is the later arrest of the secondary oocyte near ovulation, usually lifted at fertilisation.
notes.D: Dictyotene is the prolonged diplotene stage of prophase I. It is not a subdivision of meiosis II.
notes.E: Leptotene is an early subdivision of prophase I. The prolonged fetal arrest occurs later, after homologues have paired.

ana-emb-eg24-107-p18.why: Follicular granulosa cells help maintain prophase I arrest of the primary oocyte. Their signalling sustains oocyte cyclic nucleotide levels until luteinising hormone changes communication within the follicle.

notes.A: Primordial germ cells are early migratory precursors. The inhibitory signals arise from the somatic cells in the established follicle.
notes.B: Oogonia are fetal germ cells that proliferate before entering meiosis. They do not form the granulosa layer.
notes.C: Primary oocytes receive signals from their surrounding granulosa cells. Their own cyclic nucleotide pathways participate in the response.
notes.D: A secondary oocyte has already completed meiosis I. It pauses at metaphase II through a different arrest mechanism.

ana-emb-eg24-110-p18.why: The ovulated secondary oocyte usually remains capable of fertilisation for roughly one day. It loses competence if sperm do not reach it during this relatively short interval.

notes.A: Three days exceeds the usual fertilisable life of the oocyte. Sperm can remain viable for several days in favourable conditions.
notes.C: One or two hours is too short for the usual oocyte interval. Fertilisation can occur later within the first day.
notes.D: Fourteen days approximates a typical luteal phase, which is far longer than postovulatory oocyte viability.
notes.E: Sixty-four days is measured on the scale of weeks and is unrelated to the brief fertilisable life of an ovulated oocyte.

ana-emb-eg24-134-p22.why: After fertilisation, oocyte cortical granules modify the zona pellucida and reduce further sperm entry. This contribution to the polyspermy block helps preserve the usual single paternal chromosome set.

notes.B: Pronuclear development occurs after gamete fusion. The zona modification is an extracellular defence against further sperm entry.
notes.C: Oocyte activation and intracellular calcium signalling promote completion of meiosis II. The zona change is a downstream response.
notes.D: The polyspermy block is correct. The added claim about stimulating pronuclear fusion does not describe the function of the zona reaction.
notes.E: The zona reaction restricts further sperm entry. Completion of meiosis II is triggered by activation of the oocyte.

ana-emb-eg24-136-p23.why: The placenta has a fetal component formed by persistent villous chorion, the chorion frondosum, and a maternal component from decidua basalis beneath the implantation site.

notes.A: Decidua capsularis covers the conceptus toward the uterine cavity. The maternal placental bed is the decidua underneath it.
notes.B: Decidua basalis forms the maternal placental component. The fetal villous chorion supplies the other component.
notes.C: Chorion frondosum provides the fetal contribution with persistent branching villi. It develops in contact with maternal decidua basalis.
notes.D: Decidua basalis belongs to the placenta, but decidua capsularis covers the opposite side and does not supply the fetal villi.

ana-emb-eg24-144-p24.why: Unequal meiotic divisions conserve most cytoplasm in one functional oocyte. The other products are small polar bodies that contain expelled chromosome sets and do not become additional functional gametes.

notes.B: Meiosis I produces two unequal products. Only the larger daughter is a secondary oocyte, while the smaller daughter is a polar body.
notes.C: Polar bodies receive chromosomes and little cytoplasm. They therefore do not count as additional mature oocytes.
notes.D: Four functional haploid cells are characteristic of a completed spermatogenic lineage from one primary spermatocyte. Oogenesis retains one large gamete.
notes.E: A single functional cell is produced by normal maturation, so the resulting number is represented among the choices.

ana-emb-eg24-150-p25.why: Sertoli cells organise the seminiferous epithelium, form its barrier, and support and release developing germ cells. They secrete luminal fluid and androgen-binding protein and clear residual cytoplasm.

notes.A: The barrier and spermatid release are both supported by Sertoli cells. The selection omits secretion and phagocytic functions.
notes.B: The barrier, germ-cell release and androgen-binding protein are all relevant. Sertoli cells also clear residual material and provide fluid.
notes.C: Androgen-binding protein, phagocytosis and fluid production are included. The barrier and spermatid release also depend on Sertoli cells.
notes.D: The barrier, spermatid release and luminal fluid are correct. Androgen-binding protein secretion and phagocytosis are additional functions.

ana-emb-eg24-169-p29.why: Gestational age is conventionally counted from the first day of the last menstrual period. The expected duration is about 40 weeks, typically about 38 weeks from fertilisation.

notes.A: Thirty-four weeks is preterm in obstetric dating. It is shorter than the expected 40-week duration from the last menstrual period.
notes.B: About 38 weeks is the typical interval from fertilisation. Menstrual dating starts roughly two weeks earlier in a typical cycle.
notes.D: Forty-two completed weeks mark the usual threshold for post-term classification. They do not represent the average duration.
notes.E: Adding nine calendar months alone does not give the conventional 280-day estimate. Calendar months vary in length.

ana-emb-sj-oog.why: Primary oocytes enter meiosis before birth and pause in prophase I. A cyclic cohort can grow, but usually one dominant follicle releases a secondary oocyte after the luteinising hormone surge.

notes.A: Primordial follicles enclose primary oocytes that have entered meiosis and arrested in prophase I.
notes.B: Primordial follicles can be lost from the ovarian reserve. Atresia also affects growing follicles throughout life.
notes.C: Early follicle growth can occur before puberty. Regular ovulatory cycles are established later.
notes.D: Granulosa cells aromatise theca-derived androgens to oestrogens as antral follicles develop.
notes.E: Most antral follicles contain primary oocytes. The secondary stage follows completion of meiosis I just before ovulation.
notes.F: The released oocyte normally pauses in metaphase II. Meiosis II is completed after activation by fertilisation.
notes.G: A secondary oocyte and associated cumulus cells leave the dominant follicle at ovulation.
notes.H: The mid-cycle luteinising hormone surge triggers ovulation. Follicle-stimulating hormone promotes follicular growth earlier.
notes.I: Oogonia proliferate and enter meiosis during fetal development, before the primordial follicle reserve is established.
notes.J: Several follicles can grow within a recruited cohort. Selection usually leaves one dominant follicle.
notes.K: Usually one dominant follicle reaches ovulation. The other recruited follicles commonly undergo atresia.
notes.L: Combined oral contraceptives generally suppress gonadotrophin-dependent follicular development and the ovulatory surge. They do not promote maturation.

ana-emb-sa-b-19.why: Combined oral contraceptive steroids exert negative feedback on the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis. Reduced gonadotrophin stimulation and suppression of the luteinising hormone surge help prevent ovulation.

notes.A: Withdrawal bleeding can still occur during a hormone-free interval. Ovulation suppression is the principal mechanism targeted by this choice.
notes.B: Changes in cervical mucus can impede sperm passage. The pill does not act by directly blocking the sperm acrosome reaction.
notes.C: The zona reaction follows oocyte activation after fertilisation. Oral contraceptive hormones act upstream to reduce the chance of ovulation.
notes.E: Orgasm is not a target of oral contraceptive action. The relevant hormonal effects involve the reproductive endocrine axis.

ana-emb-sa-e-108.why: During gastrulation, epiblast cells move through the primitive streak and take up new positions. These coordinated movements establish the three germ layers and the embryonic body plan.

notes.A: Implantation attaches the blastocyst to endometrium and includes trophoblast invasion. The germ-layer-forming movements are a distinct embryonic event.
notes.B: Fertilisation unites the gametes and activates the oocyte. It precedes the later redistribution of epiblast cells.
notes.C: The acrosomal reaction involves changes in the sperm head that help it interact with the oocyte’s extracellular coverings.
notes.D: Decidualisation is differentiation of maternal endometrial stroma, not rearrangement of embryonic epiblast into germ layers.

ana-emb-sa-i-2.why: After oocyte activation, cortical granules modify the zona pellucida around the oocyte. This reduces further sperm binding and penetration and contributes to the block to polyspermy.

notes.A: Nidation means implantation in the endometrium and occurs after cleavage, several days after fertilisation.
notes.C: Capacitation prepares sperm for fertilisation through membrane and signalling changes. It acts before the polyspermy block.
notes.D: Acrosomal exocytosis is a sperm event that assists fertilisation. The zona modification is an oocyte response after activation.
notes.E: Ejaculation releases semen into the reproductive tract. It does not modify the egg coat after a sperm enters.

ana-emb-sa-i-9.why: Oligozoospermia means a low concentration of spermatozoa in semen. It describes a measurable semen parameter without specifying the cause or establishing whether conception is possible.

notes.A: Azoospermia means no sperm are found in the ejaculate. In this stem, a small number of sperm are present.
notes.C: Infertility is a broader clinical diagnosis. A low sperm concentration is one possible contributor and has its own term.
notes.D: Erectile dysfunction describes difficulty attaining or maintaining an erection. It does not specify the sperm count in semen.
notes.E: The semen finding has a specific name. The other terms describe absence of sperm, broader fertility status or erectile function.

ana-emb-sa-i-37.why: Zona pellucida glycoproteins help sperm interact with the oocyte’s outer coat. ZP3 is involved in classical models, while evidence in humans also supports important roles for other zona proteins.

notes.A: Hyaluronidase contributes to passage through the hyaluronan-rich cumulus matrix. It is not an egg-coat recognition glycoprotein.
notes.B: Acrosin is an acrosomal protease involved during sperm passage. The zona glycoprotein provides the proposed interaction site.
notes.C: Neuraminidase acts on terminal sialic acid residues. It is not the zona glycoprotein implicated in this sperm-binding choice.
notes.E: The zona reaction is the alteration of the coat after oocyte activation, which reduces further sperm interaction.

ana-emb-sa-i-38.why: Capacitation involves changes to the sperm plasma membrane, including loss or rearrangement of surface components. These changes prime sperm for hyperactivated motility and a later acrosomal reaction.

notes.B: Membrane fusion and vesiculation are features of the later acrosomal reaction. Capacitation prepares the sperm to undergo it.
notes.C: Proteases are released during acrosomal exocytosis. Capacitation is a preparatory process before that release.
notes.D: Acrosomal cap changes occur with acrosomal exocytosis, after the sperm has acquired competence to respond.
notes.E: The sperm retains its flagellum during capacitation. Signalling changes help it move with a hyperactivated motility pattern.

ana-emb-sa-j-12.why: Growing follicles increase in size, gain granulosa cells and develop the zona pellucida and antrum. The theca interna differentiates and supports steroid production during the growing stages.

notes.A: As antral follicles mature, follicular fluid accumulates and the cavity enlarges, displacing the oocyte towards the edge.
notes.B: The size of the follicle increases with granulosa growth, thecal differentiation and later accumulation of follicular fluid.
notes.D: Proliferation of granulosa cells expands the layer surrounding the oocyte and later the wall around the antrum.
notes.E: The zona pellucida appears around the growing oocyte as an extracellular glycoprotein layer.

ana-emb-es-37.why: Fusion of the sperm and oocyte membranes initiates oocyte activation and intracellular calcium signals. Cortical granule release then modifies the zona pellucida to limit further sperm entry.

notes.B: Interactions with the cumulus can influence sperm behaviour, but cortical granule release follows activation within the oocyte.
notes.C: Passage through the corona radiata occurs before the sperm reaches the oocyte membrane and before the cortical response.
notes.D: A sperm first passes through the zona pellucida. Oocyte activation follows fusion with the oocyte membrane beyond the zona.
notes.E: The male pronucleus forms after activation and cortical granule exocytosis have already begun.

ana-emb-eg24-37-p6.why: Capacitation remodels the sperm plasma membrane and signalling pathways after ejaculation. Loss or rearrangement of surface material over the acrosome helps prepare sperm for fertilisation.

notes.A: The zona reaction modifies the oocyte’s glycoprotein coat after activation. It occurs in a different cell at a later stage.
notes.B: Flagellar motion propels sperm. Membrane remodelling may change the beat pattern but is the specific process named here.
notes.C: Spermiation is release of elongated spermatids from Sertoli cells into the seminiferous tubule lumen, before epididymal passage.
notes.D: Physiological maturation is a broad description. Capacitation is the specific post-ejaculatory change to fertilising competence asked for here.

ana-emb-eg24-78-p13.why: Each listed contraceptive method has a nonzero failure rate. Effectiveness varies both with the method and with how consistently and correctly it is used.

notes.A: Condoms can break, slip or be used inconsistently. These possibilities leave a measurable pregnancy risk.
notes.B: Hormonal pills are highly effective when used correctly. Missed doses and other factors can reduce real-world effectiveness.
notes.C: Calendar methods estimate fertile days. Ovulation timing varies, so pregnancy remains possible even when users track cycles.
notes.D: Spermicides used alone have a measurable failure rate, with effectiveness depending in part on correct timing and application.

ana-emb-eg24-85-p14.why: The flagellum produces bending waves that propel the sperm. Its axonemal motor proteins generate movement, while metabolic pathways including those in the midpiece supply energy.

notes.A: The acrosome is a cap on the sperm head containing substances involved in fertilisation. It does not generate thrust.
notes.B: The head carries the condensed paternal genome and acrosome. Forward propulsion is produced by movement of the flagellum.
notes.C: The neck contains connecting structures linking the head to the flagellum. The propulsive beat runs along the flagellum.
notes.D: The midpiece contains a mitochondrial sheath and part of the flagellar apparatus. The flagellum as a whole provides propulsion.

ana-emb-eg24-104-p17.why: Removal of both testes eliminates the source of spermatozoa. If an ejaculate is produced later, it contains no sperm because accessory glands contribute fluid but cannot make germ cells.

notes.A: Aspermia is absence of an ejaculate. When fluid is obtained for analysis, absence of sperm is recorded separately.
notes.B: Globozoospermia describes abnormal round-headed sperm. There must be sperm present for this morphological finding.
notes.C: Oligozoospermia denotes a low sperm concentration with some sperm remaining. With no testes, new sperm are not produced.
notes.E: Hypospermia describes reduced semen volume. The expected sperm-specific finding after bilateral testis removal is absence of sperm.

ana-emb-eg24-131-p22.why: The rhythm or calendar method uses previous menstrual cycle lengths to estimate the fertile window. Contraceptive use depends on avoiding unprotected intercourse during the predicted fertile days.

notes.A: An intrauterine device prevents pregnancy through its actions within the reproductive tract. Routine use does not require cycle charting.
notes.B: Barrier methods physically reduce sperm passage during intercourse. Their action does not depend on predicting ovulation.
notes.D: Hormonal methods act through reproductive hormone signalling or cervical mucus changes. They are not defined by calendar tracking.
notes.E: Withdrawal requires removing the penis before ejaculation. It does not identify fertile days from the menstrual cycle.

ana-emb-eg24-132-p22.why: Contraceptive injections and implants deliver hormones that can suppress ovulation or thicken cervical mucus. Progestogens are typical, and some injectable formulations also contain oestrogen.

notes.B: A barrier physically blocks sperm. Injections and implants instead deliver a drug whose contraceptive action is hormonal.
notes.C: Implants are removable and injections wear off with time. They are intended to be reversible methods.
notes.D: Calendar methods estimate the fertile window from cycle patterns. These contraceptives act whether or not cycles are charted.
notes.E: An intrauterine device sits inside the uterus. An implant is placed under the skin and an injection is administered separately.

ana-emb-eg24-133-p22.why: Tubal sterilisation and vasectomy interrupt reproductive ducts and are intended as permanent contraception. A contraceptive implant provides long-acting hormonal contraception and can be removed.

notes.A: Tubal ligation or occlusion is a permanent method. The choice omits vasectomy, which is also intended to be permanent.
notes.B: Vasectomy interrupts sperm transport through the ductus deferens and is intended to be permanent. Tubal sterilisation also qualifies.
notes.C: The implant releases a hormone for a limited duration and can be removed when the user wants to discontinue it.
notes.D: The surgical methods meet the permanent category. The implant is a long-acting reversible method, so including it makes this combination incorrect.

ana-emb-eg24-135-p23.why: During the acrosome reaction, membranes at the anterior sperm head fuse and vesiculate. Acrosomal enzymes are released and help the sperm interact with the oocyte’s coverings.

notes.B: The acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes rather than a hormone-secreting system. Exocytosis releases its enzymatic contents.
notes.C: Acrosomal membranes are remodelled and can shed vesicles. The characteristic released soluble contents asked for are enzymes.
notes.D: Enzyme release is correct, but the additional claim of hormone release is not part of acrosomal exocytosis.
notes.E: This combination includes hormone release and omits the enzymatic contents characteristically released from the acrosome.

ana-emb-eg24-137-p23.why: Implantation usually starts about six to seven days after fertilisation. By then a hatched blastocyst can appose and attach to receptive secretory endometrium.

notes.A: At one to two days, cleavage is under way while the early embryo is still moving along the uterine tube.
notes.B: Around days two to three the embryo has several blastomeres. The enclosing zona is still usually present.
notes.C: Compaction and early blastocyst formation occur around this period. Endometrial attachment usually begins after hatching.
notes.E: By ten to twelve days implantation is usually well advanced. The first attachment takes place several days sooner.

ana-emb-sj-ivf.why: In vitro fertilisation can bypass obstructed tubes and can use retrieved, stored or donated gametes. Embryo transfer also requires a receptive uterus, which can be hormonally prepared.

notes.A: IVF brings sperm and oocytes together outside the body. Embryo transfer bypasses the blocked uterine tubes.
notes.B: Bilateral ovary removal eliminates new oocyte retrieval. Donor oocytes are needed if the patient has no previously stored oocytes or embryos.
notes.C: A person without a functional uterus cannot carry an intrauterine pregnancy. A gestational carrier can carry the transferred embryo.
notes.D: Some causes of azoospermia allow sperm retrieval from the testis or epididymis, depending on the cause and extent of sperm production.
notes.E: A low sperm count does not necessarily prevent using the patient’s sperm. Laboratory techniques can help when viable sperm are available.
notes.F: Vasectomy blocks the ductus deferens rather than sperm production. In selected cases, sperm can be retrieved for assisted fertilisation.
notes.G: A urethral obstruction can prevent semen delivery. Selected patients may have sperm retrieved upstream if spermatogenesis is intact.
notes.H: Cryopreserved sperm can be thawed and assessed for use in assisted reproduction if sufficient viable cells remain.
notes.I: Sperm can undergo the acrosome reaction in conventional IVF. Direct intracytoplasmic injection bypasses its usual role in zona penetration.
notes.J: A postmenopausal endometrium generally needs hormonal preparation for embryo transfer because it lacks the usual cyclic ovarian support.

ana-emb-sj-fert.why: Sperm–oocyte fusion activates the secondary oocyte, modifies its coat and completes meiosis II. Combining the parental genomes establishes the zygote and enables the first cleavage divisions.

notes.A: Oocyte activation releases cortical granules that modify the zona pellucida and limit additional sperm entry.
notes.B: The fertilising sperm usually contributes either an X or a Y chromosome, establishing the zygote’s sex chromosome complement.
notes.C: The acrosome reaction occurs in the sperm before membrane fusion and helps enable interaction with the oocyte’s extracellular coverings.
notes.D: Meiosis I normally finishes just before ovulation. Fertilisation activates completion of the second meiotic division.
notes.E: Activation allows the metaphase II-arrested oocyte to separate sister chromatids and extrude its second polar body.
notes.F: Oocyte activation initiates development leading to cleavage, the mitotic division sequence of the new embryo.
notes.G: The fusion and activation events establish the fertilised single cell known as the zygote.
notes.H: Formation of a blastocyst requires several days of cleavage and organisation after the zygote has formed.
notes.I: Combining independently assorted and recombined maternal and paternal genomes creates a new genetic combination in the zygote.
notes.J: The second polar body is expelled. The maternal chromosome set retained in the oocyte forms the female pronucleus.

ana-emb-sj-inf.why: Infertility can reflect problems with intercourse, delivery or function of gametes, and passage through reproductive ducts. Clinical effect depends on the specific site, severity and associated findings.

notes.A: An undescended testis in infancy needs follow-up, but this finding alone does not establish adult infertility, particularly if the other testis is normal.
notes.B: Pelvic infection can scar the uterine tubes, preventing gametes from meeting or impairing embryo transport.
notes.C: Genital infection can alter secretions or cause inflammation that impairs sperm passage. General vaginal acidity alone is not a diagnosis.
notes.D: Erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction can prevent effective deposition of semen even when sperm production is intact.
notes.E: Severe obesity can affect ovulation and other reproductive functions through endocrine and metabolic mechanisms.
notes.F: Absent ejaculation can prevent sperm delivery to the female reproductive tract even if sperm are produced.
notes.G: Female orgasm is not required for sperm deposition, fertilisation or normal implantation.
notes.H: An obstructed vaginal outlet can prevent penetrative intercourse or access to the cervix, depending on the anatomy.
notes.I: A single length threshold does not determine whether intercourse or semen deposition is possible.
notes.J: Kartagener syndrome is a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia. It can impair sperm flagellar motility.
notes.K: Fallopian tube ciliary dysfunction can impair gamete or embryo transport in those with primary ciliary dyskinesia.
