notes.L: Abnormally thick or poorly penetrable cervical mucus can impede sperm passage, although clinically significant cervical-factor infertility is uncommon.
notes.M: Ductal scarring can obstruct delivery of sperm from the male reproductive tract into the urethra.
notes.N: The female urethra is a urinary passage. Obstruction there is not itself a blockage of the sperm or oocyte route.

ana-emb-sa-b-13.why: The embryoblast separates into epiblast and hypoblast. The hypoblast is the early layer called primitive endoderm, which contributes to yolk-sac lining rather than the definitive embryonic gut.

notes.A: The amnion develops around the early amniotic cavity adjacent to the epiblast. It is a membrane rather than the primitive endodermal layer.
notes.B: The chorion combines trophoblast and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm. It does not arise as the first embryoblast layer.
notes.D: Definitive embryonic ectoderm is derived from the epiblast during gastrulation, after the bilaminar disc has formed.
notes.E: Intraembryonic mesoderm forms when epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak during gastrulation.

ana-emb-sa-i-27.why: The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated trophoblast layer at early implantation. It penetrates the endometrium and forms the early interface with surrounding maternal tissue.

notes.A: The embryoblast is the inner cell mass that forms the embryonic disc. Maternal contact is made by the overlying trophoblast.
notes.B: The amniotic membrane surrounds the forming cavity next to the epiblast. It lies within the conceptus.
notes.C: The primary yolk sac forms toward the hypoblast inside the conceptus. It is not the invasive maternal interface.
notes.D: Cytotrophoblast is the inner cellular trophoblast layer that supplies cells to the overlying syncytium during initial implantation.

ana-emb-sa-i-28.why: The embryoblast, or inner cell mass, gives rise to the epiblast and hypoblast. These layers form the early bilaminar embryonic disc before the primitive streak develops.

notes.B: Trophoblast derives from the outer cells of the early blastocyst, whereas the embryoblast is its inner cell population.
notes.C: Extraembryonic mesoderm develops later around embryonic cavities. It is not one of the initial layers formed directly by segregation of the embryoblast.
notes.D: Intraembryonic mesoderm comes from epiblast cells passing through the primitive streak during gastrulation, after the bilaminar disc stage.
notes.E: The epiblast is a direct derivative of the embryoblast and is included among the choices.

ana-emb-sa-i-32.why: Implantation begins when the blastocyst hatches and attaches to receptive endometrium. Its outer trophoblast then differentiates and invades the uterine lining.

notes.A: The zygote is the single cell immediately after fertilisation and is still in the uterine tube at this stage.
notes.B: A sixteen-cell embryo is usually at or approaching the morula stage, before the blastocyst forms and hatches.
notes.C: Cell number alone does not define readiness for implantation. A cavitated, hatched blastocyst attaches through its trophoblast.
notes.E: The bilaminar disc describes differentiation within the embryoblast during early implantation. The whole conceptus attaches as a blastocyst.

ana-emb-sa-i-33.why: Loss of the zona pellucida lets the blastocyst’s trophoblast contact the receptive endometrium directly. This hatching step enables the apposition and adhesion that start implantation.

notes.B: Endometrial decidual changes support implantation. Hatching is the immediate physical prerequisite that exposes the trophoblast for contact.
notes.C: The inner and outer cell populations segregate earlier as the blastocyst forms. The surrounding coat still has to be shed.
notes.D: The other processes contribute to development or uterine response, but neither substitutes for exposing the trophoblast by hatching.
notes.E: Zona shedding opens access to the endometrial surface, so a recognised prerequisite is present among the choices.

ana-emb-sa-i-34.why: The blastocyst attaches during the postovulatory secretory phase. Progesterone from the corpus luteum makes the endometrial glands secretory and helps establish a receptive implantation window.

notes.A: The proliferative phase precedes ovulation and is driven mainly by oestrogen. Implantation usually starts after the luteal phase begins.
notes.B: Decidualisation can begin in the secretory phase and intensifies around implantation. Secretory is the cycle phase asked for here.
notes.D: The postovulatory secretory phase is a standard term and is included among the choices.
notes.E: The endometrium is not in every listed phase. Progesterone-dependent secretory maturation precedes attachment.

ana-emb-es-40.why: Monozygotic twins form when one early conceptus separates into two embryonic lineages. In the classical model, the time of separation influences which fetal membranes are shared.

notes.A: Separation of the inner embryonic population at the blastocyst stage is classically associated with a shared chorion.
notes.B: Very early cleavage-stage separation can produce two separate blastocysts with their own chorions and amnions.
notes.C: Cells can also separate at the morula stage, before a single chorion has been established.
notes.D: The conventional model places ordinary complete twinning earlier. Very late incomplete separation is sometimes invoked to explain conjoined twinning.
notes.E: Neurulation follows early axis formation and is well beyond the usual time assigned to separation into two embryos.

ana-emb-eg24-22-p4.why: Most ectopic pregnancies implant in a uterine tube, particularly its ampullary region. Tubal implantation occurs before the blastocyst reaches the usual site in the uterine cavity.

notes.A: Cervical implantation is a recognised but uncommon form of ectopic pregnancy. Tubal locations are substantially more frequent.
notes.B: The ovary can be an ectopic implantation site, but ovarian pregnancies account for a small minority of ectopic pregnancies.
notes.C: An abdominal implant occurs outside the uterine cavity and tube. It is less frequent than tubal implantation.
notes.E: The uterine tube is the most common ectopic site, and it appears explicitly among the options.

ana-emb-eg24-26-p4.why: As the morula compacts, outer cells adopt trophectoderm identity and inner cells form the embryoblast. The outer lineage supplies the trophoblast of the developing blastocyst.

notes.A: The amnion forms later around the cavity adjacent to the epiblast, after the primary outer and inner lineages separate.
notes.B: The chorion is a membrane formed later from trophoblast and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm.
notes.C: The hypoblast separates later within the inner cell mass. It is not the early outer lineage of the morula.
notes.D: The epiblast is specified within the embryoblast after the outer trophectoderm lineage is established.

ana-emb-eg24-53-p9.why: Decidualisation is the progesterone-responsive transformation of endometrial stromal cells. It begins during the secretory phase and becomes more pronounced around the implanting conceptus.

notes.A: Capacitation alters sperm membranes and signalling during preparation for fertilisation. It does not describe an endometrial change.
notes.B: Gastrulation reorganises the embryonic epiblast into germ layers. Decidualisation occurs in maternal tissue.
notes.D: Nidation is implantation itself. The associated stromal transformation of the uterine lining is a separate process.
notes.E: Fertilisation unites sperm and oocyte and normally occurs in the uterine tube, before the endometrial response.

ana-emb-eg24-75-p12.why: Cleavage divides the zygote mitotically into smaller cells without corresponding overall growth. These individual cells are blastomeres, which later compact and contribute to blastocyst lineages.

notes.A: A blastocyst is the entire later structure containing a cavity and specialised cell populations. Individual cleavage cells have a different name.
notes.C: Trophoblast cells belong to an outer lineage established after early cleavage and compaction. The earlier cells are blastomeres.
notes.D: The embryoblast is the inner cell mass in the blastocyst. It represents one population descended from blastomeres.
notes.E: Only one term describes the individual products of cleavage. The other terms refer to later structures or lineages.

ana-emb-eg24-79-p13.why: Low uterine implantation can leave the placenta near the internal cervical opening. Placenta praevia is diagnosed when placental tissue overlies that opening later in pregnancy.

notes.A: Tubal implantation is an ectopic pregnancy. Placenta praevia concerns placental location in a pregnancy within the uterus.
notes.C: Fundal implantation is high in the uterus and usually places the placenta away from the internal cervical opening.
notes.D: Ovarian implantation is an ectopic pregnancy and cannot produce the usual placental relationship to the cervical opening.
notes.E: Abdominal implantation is ectopic. The relationship defining placenta praevia occurs within the lower uterus.

ana-emb-eg24-121-p20.why: Fertilisation establishes a single-cell zygote containing maternal and paternal chromosome sets. Its pronuclear envelopes later break down so the chromosomes can participate in the first mitosis.

notes.A: The first polar body is produced when the primary oocyte completes meiosis I. It forms before the paternal genome enters.
notes.B: The second polar body results from completion of meiosis II after activation. It does not retain both parental genomes.
notes.C: A pronucleus contains one parental chromosome set before the first zygotic mitosis. The whole fertilised cell is the zygote.
notes.E: A blastomere is produced when the zygote starts cleavage. It is a daughter cell rather than the initial fertilised cell.

ana-emb-eg24-170-p29.why: The syncytiotrophoblast secretes human chorionic gonadotrophin after implantation begins. The hormone maintains the early corpus luteum and thereby sustains progesterone production until placental production increases.

notes.B: Decidua basalis is maternal endometrial tissue beneath the implant. The syncytiotrophoblast contributes to the fetal placental component.
notes.C: Around day four the conceptus is usually at the morula or early blastocyst transition. Invasive syncytium appears with implantation.
notes.D: The zona pellucida is the surrounding glycoprotein coat that is shed before implantation. Syncytiotrophoblast is derived from trophoblast.
notes.E: The villous syncytiotrophoblast remains present and provides an exchange and endocrine surface. Cytotrophoblast cells replenish it by fusion.

ana-emb-sj-dz.why: Dizygotic twins arise when two separate oocytes are fertilised. Each twin usually has a separate chorion, amnion and cord, although adjacent placental discs can fuse.

notes.A: Each oocyte is fertilised separately, so there are two zygotes rather than separation of one zygote.
notes.B: Dizygotic twins are genetically comparable to other full siblings. Each inherits a different combination of parental alleles.
notes.C: Two adjacent placental discs can join and appear as one mass, while the pregnancy remains dichorionic.
notes.D: Dizygotic twins ordinarily form separate amniotic sacs because they originate from two separate conceptuses.
notes.E: Two oocytes may be released from follicles in the same ovary within one ovulatory cycle.
notes.F: Ovulatory follicles in both ovaries can release oocytes that are subsequently fertilised in the same cycle.
notes.G: The two fertilisations are independent. The twins can have the same or different sex chromosome complements.
notes.H: Each fetus has its own umbilical cord, even when the outer placental discs are fused.

ana-emb-sj-impl.why: A hatched blastocyst attaches at its embryonic pole to secretory endometrium. Trophoblast invades at that site, where persistent villi form the chorion frondosum against decidua basalis.

notes.A: The zona pellucida is shed before attachment, exposing the trophoblast so it can contact the endometrial surface.
notes.B: The morula is an earlier solid cell mass. Implantation begins after blastocyst formation and hatching.
notes.C: Attachment usually begins on the side of the blastocyst containing the embryoblast, known as the embryonic pole.
notes.D: Decidua basalis lies deep to the conceptus toward the myometrium. Capsularis covers the opposite side.
notes.E: Decidua capsularis faces the uterine cavity. Decidua basalis lies beneath the site of implantation.
notes.F: Villi regress on the capsular side, producing smooth chorion, or chorion laeve, against the decidua capsularis.
notes.G: Branching villi persist at the maternal placental bed, which is decidua basalis rather than the parietal lining.
notes.H: Implantation begins in progesterone-conditioned secretory endometrium during the postovulatory phase.
notes.I: The endometrium undergoes further decidual change after attachment. It does not return to its preovulatory proliferative state.
notes.J: Syncytiotrophoblast is the outer invasive layer and directly contacts surrounding maternal tissue at the implantation site.

ana-emb-sa-a-3.why: The amnion includes amniotic epithelium with a supporting outer layer of extraembryonic somatic mesoderm. This layer is also called somatopleuric mesoderm.

notes.A: Extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm covers the yolk sac. The mesoderm applied to the amnion is the somatic layer.
notes.C: Lateral plate terminology describes a broader somatic and splanchnic distinction. The specific extraembryonic layer at the amnion is somatic.
notes.D: Intermediate mesoderm contributes to the urogenital system. It does not supply the amniotic supporting layer.
notes.E: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites and their axial derivatives. It is distinct from extraembryonic mesoderm at the amnion.

ana-emb-sa-a-5.why: The epiblast faces the developing amniotic cavity and forms its embryonic floor. After gastrulation, surface ectoderm derived from epiblast occupies the corresponding dorsal embryonic surface.

notes.A: The amniotic membrane forms the roof and outer lining around the cavity. The embryonic floor is formed by the disc surface.
notes.B: Intraembryonic mesoderm forms after gastrulation and lies beneath ectoderm, rather than directly facing the amniotic cavity.
notes.C: Extraembryonic mesoderm supports the outer amnion. It does not form the surface of the embryonic disc facing the cavity.
notes.E: Endoderm is on the ventral side of the embryonic disc, facing the yolk sac rather than the amniotic cavity.

ana-emb-sa-a-6.why: The expanding amnion encloses the connecting stalk and vitelline connection to help form the cord. A small coelomic space within it can temporarily contain physiologically herniated midgut.

notes.A: A temporary extension of the extraembryonic coelom persists near the cord base and can receive midgut during physiological herniation.
notes.B: The amnion covers the outside of the cord. The amniotic cavity and its fluid surround the cord rather than lying inside it.
notes.C: The vitelline duct and associated yolk-sac remnants can lie within the early cord near the embryonic attachment.
notes.D: The intervillous space is a placental compartment containing maternal blood around the chorionic villi. It is outside the cord.
notes.E: Chorion forms the outer fetal membrane and the fetal side of the placenta. Amnion supplies the surface covering of the cord.

ana-emb-sa-a-7.why: The growing amniotic sac expands until the amnion comes into contact with and fuses to the chorion. This eliminates the intervening chorionic cavity, or extraembryonic coelom.

notes.A: The yolk sac regresses as development progresses. It is a separate sac rather than the cavity between amnion and chorion.
notes.B: Trophoblastic lacunae coalesce to form the maternal intervillous space. Amniotic expansion closes a different compartment.
notes.C: The blastocyst is an earlier developmental stage. Its cavity has already been remodelled before the amnion expands to the chorion.
notes.E: Decidual surfaces come together as the conceptus expands, but the amnion directly eliminates the space inside the chorion.

ana-emb-sa-b-9.why: The placenta secretes human chorionic gonadotrophin, placental lactogen and steroid hormones during pregnancy. Luteinising hormone is secreted by gonadotrophs in the anterior pituitary.

notes.B: Syncytiotrophoblast produces human chorionic gonadotrophin, which supports the early corpus luteum through the luteinising hormone receptor.
notes.C: Human chorionic somatomammotrophin is also called placental lactogen. It is a major syncytiotrophoblast product.
notes.D: The placenta is the main source of progesterone after the luteal–placental shift in early pregnancy.
notes.E: Placental enzymes synthesise oestrogens from androgen precursors supplied by maternal and fetal tissues.

ana-emb-sa-b-17.why: Human chorionic gonadotrophin from the early trophoblast activates luteinising hormone receptors on luteal cells. It prevents early luteal regression and sustains progesterone production until placental output is adequate.

notes.B: Placental thyrotrophic activity concerns thyroid stimulation. Early corpus luteum rescue is mediated by circulating chorionic gonadotrophin.
notes.C: Human placental lactogen contributes to maternal metabolic and mammary adaptations. It is not the principal early luteal rescue signal.
notes.D: Follicle-stimulating hormone supports recruitment and growth of follicles. It does not provide the main pregnancy signal to the corpus luteum.
notes.E: Luteinising hormone supports the ordinary menstrual corpus luteum. During early pregnancy human chorionic gonadotrophin maintains it.

ana-emb-sa-e-113.why: Decidua basalis is maternal endometrium at the placental bed. The fetal component develops from chorion frondosum, where chorionic villi continue to grow and branch.

notes.B: Capsularis covers the conceptus toward the uterine cavity, and chorion laeve is the smooth chorion facing it.
notes.C: Decidua parietalis and capsularis are both maternal regions. Neither supplies the fetal villous component of the placenta.
notes.D: Chorion laeve is fetal smooth chorion, while decidua parietalis is maternal tissue away from the early placental bed.
notes.E: Decidua basalis is the correct maternal component. The fetal contribution comes from villous rather than smooth chorion.

ana-emb-sa-i-8.why: Luteinising hormone is a pituitary gonadotrophin. The placenta produces related human chorionic gonadotrophin and contributes steroid, peptide and regulatory products to the maternal–fetal endocrine system.

notes.A: Older endocrine accounts describe placental chorionic thyrotrophic activity. This terminology refers to thyroid-stimulating activity rather than pituitary luteinising hormone.
notes.C: The placenta and decidua contribute inhibin during pregnancy, particularly later when placental endocrine output increases.
notes.D: The placenta produces oestrogens by aromatising androgen precursors from maternal and fetal sources.
notes.E: The corpus luteum is a major source of circulating relaxin, but relaxin is also identified in placental and decidual tissues.

ana-emb-sa-i-13.why: The decidua basalis is the portion of maternal endometrium beneath the implanted conceptus. It forms the maternal placental bed against the developing fetal chorionic villi.

notes.B: Decidua capsularis covers the implanted conceptus on the side facing the uterine cavity rather than underlying the placental bed.
notes.C: Decidua parietalis is the lining of the uterine cavity away from the initial implantation site.
notes.D: Chorion laeve is a fetal membrane with regressed villi. It is not maternal endometrium.
notes.E: Chorion frondosum is the fetal villous portion of the placenta, paired with maternal decidua basalis.

ana-emb-sa-i-14.why: Chorion frondosum retains branching villi adjacent to decidua basalis and forms the fetal side of the placenta. On the opposite side, the villi regress.

notes.B: Chorion laeve is the smooth portion of the fetal chorion where the villi have regressed.
notes.C: Decidua capsularis is maternal endometrium over the conceptus toward the uterine cavity. It is not the fetal placenta.
notes.D: Decidua parietalis is maternal endometrial lining away from the implantation site. It is not a chorionic tissue.
notes.E: Decidua basalis supplies the maternal placental component. The fetal villi arise from adjacent chorion frondosum.

ana-emb-sa-i-23.why: The chorion is the outer fetal membrane. It consists of extraembryonic somatic mesoderm next to the inner cytotrophoblast and the external syncytiotrophoblast.

notes.A: Extraembryonic somatic mesoderm forms the connective tissue component. The chorion also includes both trophoblast layers.
notes.B: Cytotrophoblast supplies the cellular trophoblast layer. It forms the chorion together with syncytium and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm.
notes.C: Syncytiotrophoblast is the external multinucleated layer. It is one of three components in the early chorionic structure.
notes.E: All three listed tissues contribute when the mesoderm is specified as the extraembryonic somatic layer.

ana-emb-sa-i-29.why: The chorionic cavity expands through extraembryonic mesoderm around the amnion and yolk sac. The connecting stalk remains a solid bridge linking the embryonic region to the chorion.

notes.A: The coelom lies outside the amnion and surrounds its exposed surface as the chorionic cavity expands.
notes.B: The yolk sac projects into the chorionic cavity and is covered externally by extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm.
notes.C: The bilaminar disc lies between amnion and yolk sac. It is connected to the outer chorion at the residual stalk.
notes.D: Gastrulation creates the trilaminar disc later. The persistent mesodermal connection defining the interruption is the stalk.

ana-emb-sa-i-30.why: Extraembryonic mesoderm occupies the region between trophoblast and embryonic sacs. Spaces coalesce within this mesoderm to create the chorionic cavity, which is distinct from the original blastocoele.

notes.A: Embryonic ectoderm differentiates from epiblast later during gastrulation. It does not form the tissue in which the chorionic spaces open.
notes.B: Intraembryonic mesoderm forms within the embryonic disc later. The early chorionic cavity develops in extraembryonic tissue.
notes.D: Hypoblast-derived endoderm lines the early yolk sac. The layer that cavitates to form the chorionic cavity is extraembryonic mesoderm.
notes.E: The relevant mesodermal population is explicitly listed and occupies the space around the early embryonic sacs.

ana-emb-es-39.why: Epiblast cells form the primitive streak and migrate through it during gastrulation in the third week. They produce definitive endoderm and mesoderm, while remaining epiblast becomes ectoderm.

notes.A: The amniotic cavity is a fluid space above the disc. Its lining does not supply all three embryonic germ layers.
notes.B: Cytotrophoblast contributes to placental development. Gastrulation is driven by cell movements within the embryonic epiblast.
notes.D: Hypoblast contributes mainly to extraembryonic yolk-sac lining. Definitive embryonic endoderm is derived from migrating epiblast.
notes.E: The primary yolk sac is an extraembryonic structure. The major third-week reorganisation of the embryo occurs in the disc.

ana-emb-es-42.why: The fluid released when the waters break is contained within the amniotic cavity. The membranes around the fetus rupture and allow amniotic fluid to escape.

notes.B: The chorionic cavity is the early space outside the amnion. It is largely eliminated as the amnion expands and fuses with chorion.
notes.C: The allantois is a small outgrowth associated with the connecting stalk. It is not the sac of fluid around the fetus.
notes.D: The yolk sac serves early developmental functions and is separate from the fluid-filled cavity surrounding the fetus.
notes.E: The uterine cavity is the maternal space in which the pregnancy develops. Amniotic fluid is enclosed inside the fetal membranes.

ana-emb-es-43.why: Amniotic fluid cushions the developing fetus and permits free movement while limiting direct membrane contact. It also helps maintain a stable thermal and mechanical environment.

notes.A: Fluid distributes external pressure and helps protect the fetus from mechanical shocks.
notes.B: The surrounding fluid gives the fetus room to move, supporting symmetrical growth and development.
notes.C: The fluid-filled environment limits rapid temperature shifts and helps protect the fetus from external thermal changes.
notes.D: Fluid separates fetal surfaces from the amnion, reducing prolonged contact that could lead to adhesions.

ana-emb-es-44.why: Wharton’s jelly is a hydrated, mucous connective tissue formed from extraembryonic mesenchyme in the umbilical cord. It supports the vessels and helps protect them from compression.

notes.A: Paraxial mesoderm forms embryonic somites and axial musculoskeletal derivatives. It does not supply the cord’s supporting jelly.
notes.B: Intermediate mesoderm contributes to renal and reproductive primordia. The cord stroma forms in an extraembryonic compartment.
notes.C: Embryonic lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body wall and visceral structures. Wharton’s jelly is derived from extraembryonic mesoderm.
notes.E: Syncytiotrophoblast forms part of the placental interface. The core connective tissue in the cord is mesenchymal.

ana-emb-eg24-47-p8.why: The late placental exchange barrier becomes locally thin as fetal capillaries approach the syncytiotrophoblast. Villous cytotrophoblast is discontinuous and is absent at many of these thin exchange sites.

notes.A: Fetal capillary endothelium lines the fetal blood compartment and remains part of the barrier during late pregnancy.
notes.C: The fetal endothelial basal lamina remains present and can closely approach the trophoblastic basal lamina.
notes.D: The trophoblastic basal lamina remains at thin sites and may lie closely apposed to the capillary basal lamina.
notes.E: Syncytiotrophoblast remains the outer fetal layer in contact with maternal blood and participates directly in exchange.

ana-emb-eg24-52-p9.why: The chorion combines cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm. The splanchnic layer of extraembryonic mesoderm instead covers the yolk sac.

notes.A: Cytotrophoblast is the inner cellular trophoblast layer and forms part of early chorionic tissue.
notes.B: Syncytiotrophoblast forms the multinucleated external trophoblast layer and contributes to the chorion.
notes.C: Extraembryonic somatic mesoderm lies against trophoblast and forms the chorion’s supporting connective tissue.
notes.E: One listed mesodermal layer belongs to the yolk-sac side of the extraembryonic coelom rather than the chorion.

ana-emb-eg24-61-p10.why: Urine pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotrophin produced by trophoblast after implantation begins. Its concentration rises in maternal blood and subsequently becomes detectable in urine.

notes.A: Human chorionic somatomammotrophin is placental lactogen. It contributes to maternal adaptation but is not the routine urine test target.
notes.B: Chorionic thyrotrophic activity relates to the thyroid axis. Standard urine pregnancy tests target chorionic gonadotrophin.
notes.D: Luteinising hormone is a pituitary hormone measured in ovulation prediction. Pregnancy urine assays are designed to detect chorionic gonadotrophin.
notes.E: Relaxin participates in pregnancy physiology. It is not the hormone detected in standard urine pregnancy testing.

ana-emb-eg24-161-p28.why: In normal placental separation, uterine contraction helps shear the placenta from the wall through the spongy portion of decidua basalis. The deeper regenerative tissue remains.

notes.A: The deepest basal tissue is retained for endometrial regeneration. The normal cleavage plane is in the more superficial spongy layer.
notes.B: The compact layer is the denser superficial region. The separation plane is in the looser spongy decidua below it.
notes.D: Separation is normally localised to a plane within the spongy layer. The decidual layers do not all split as a unit.
notes.E: The characteristic separation plane is present among the choices and lies within the spongy portion of the decidua.

ana-emb-sj-prog.why: Placental progesterone supports the decidual endometrium and helps maintain uterine quiescence. It also acts on the cervix, reproductive endocrine axis and mammary glands during pregnancy.

notes.A: Routine urine pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotrophin. Progesterone is not the hormone targeted by these tests.
notes.B: Progesterone supports the secretory and decidual changes that maintain the uterine lining during pregnancy.
notes.C: Progesterone helps keep the myometrium relatively quiescent and limits pathways that promote contractions.
notes.D: High pregnancy steroid concentrations contribute negative feedback to the hypothalamic–pituitary axis, reducing pituitary gonadotrophin secretion.
notes.E: Progesterone supports thick, viscous cervical secretions that help form the cervical mucus plug.
notes.F: Progesterone helps maintain pregnancy and cervical stability. Cervical ripening near labour involves a change in local signalling and tissue remodelling.
notes.G: Progesterone contributes to mammary lobuloalveolar development in combination with other pregnancy hormones.
notes.H: High progesterone restrains copious milk secretion during pregnancy. Its fall after placental delivery helps permit secretory activation.
notes.I: Circulating progesterone remains high into late pregnancy. Labour in humans involves changes in functional responsiveness before levels fall after delivery.
notes.J: Progesterone receptor blockade can disrupt progesterone-dependent decidual support and is used in some approaches to pregnancy termination.

ana-emb-sj-hcs.why: Human placental lactogen increases as placental mass grows. It has lactogenic effects and contributes to maternal metabolic changes that make substrates available to the growing fetus.

notes.A: Human chorionic somatomammotrophin and human placental lactogen are names for the same placental hormone.
notes.B: Placental lactogen is a polypeptide with structural similarities to growth hormone and prolactin.
notes.C: Placental lactogen generally rises toward term as the placenta grows. The earlier sharp peak is characteristic of chorionic gonadotrophin.
notes.D: Placental lactogen is produced in pregnancy. Pubertal breast development occurs earlier under the influence of other endocrine signals.
notes.E: Placental lactogen contributes to reduced maternal insulin sensitivity, which helps preserve glucose availability for fetal transfer.
notes.F: It has structural and functional similarities to growth hormone. Its actions are not generally described as growth hormone antagonism.
notes.G: Its lactogenic effects contribute to mammary development in concert with prolactin and pregnancy steroids.
notes.H: It contributes to mobilisation of maternal fat, increasing availability of fatty acids as an alternative fuel.

ana-emb-sj-oes.why: Placental oestrogens contribute to uterine and vascular adaptation during pregnancy. Rising oestrogen signalling near term also promotes pathways that increase myometrial responsiveness to oxytocin.

notes.A: Progesterone and oestrogens both support aspects of pregnancy. Their actions and relative effects vary with tissue and gestational stage.
notes.B: Oestrogen signalling can increase oxytocin receptor expression in the myometrium and facilitate stronger responses near labour.
notes.C: Androgens, including locally formed dihydrotestosterone, drive typical male external genital differentiation. This is not the role described for placental oestrogens.
notes.D: Oestrogen can promote vascular adaptation and vasodilatation, contributing to increased uteroplacental perfusion.
notes.E: Placental oestrogens act in maternal and fetal compartments. The proposed fixed proportion used by the fetus is not a standard physiological description.
notes.F: High pregnancy steroid levels participate in negative feedback that suppresses maternal gonadotrophin secretion.

ana-emb-sa-a-1.why: Epiblast cells ingress through the primitive node at the cranial end of the streak. They migrate forward and form the axial notochordal process, which becomes the notochord.

notes.A: Extraembryonic mesoderm supports structures outside the disc. The notochord forms in the embryonic midline from node-derived cells.
notes.B: The node lies at the cranial end of the streak. It is the specific entry region for notochord-forming cells.
notes.D: The notochordal plate is temporarily continuous with the endodermal surface. The notochordal cells themselves arise by ingression through the node.
notes.E: The neural groove forms later in overlying neuroectoderm. The notochord is an axial structure located beneath it.

ana-emb-sa-a-2.why: At the cloacal membrane, surface ectoderm and endoderm remain in contact without interposed mesoderm. This membrane lies at the caudal end of the developing gut.

notes.A: The buccopharyngeal membrane also has direct ectoderm–endoderm contact, but it lies at the cranial end of the gut.
notes.B: The primitive knot is the node at the cranial end of the streak. Cells ingress there during gastrulation.
notes.C: The primitive streak is a site of epiblast cell ingression and supplies germ-layer progenitors. It is not the caudal closing membrane.
notes.D: The prechordal plate is a cranial midline organising region near the future oral end, away from the cloacal membrane.

ana-emb-sa-a-4.why: The notochord and nearby axial organiser tissues provide signals that help induce and pattern the overlying neuroectoderm. This region thickens into the neural plate during early development.

notes.A: Endoderm provides epithelial precursors for internal organs. The specified axial inducer beneath the developing neural plate is the notochord.
notes.C: Extraembryonic mesoderm lies outside the disc and supports fetal membranes. It is not the midline structure beneath the prospective neural plate.
notes.D: Intraembryonic mesoderm is a broad category including axial tissues. The notochord is the specific organiser named among the options.
notes.E: The primitive streak provides a route for germ-layer formation. Its cranial node gives rise to axial cells that later signal to overlying ectoderm.

ana-emb-sa-b-14.why: Paraxial mesoderm lies immediately beside the embryonic midline. It segments in a cranial-to-caudal sequence into paired somites alongside the developing neural tube.

notes.A: Lateral plate mesoderm is farther from the midline and splits around the intraembryonic coelom.
notes.C: Intermediate mesoderm lies between paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm and contributes to the urogenital system.
notes.D: Somatic lateral plate mesoderm lies next to ectoderm and contributes to the body wall and limb connective tissues.
notes.E: Splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm lies next to endoderm and contributes to visceral tissues rather than forming somites.

ana-emb-sa-e-109.why: Somites form as paraxial mesoderm segments on either side of the neural tube. Their cells later contribute to vertebrae, skeletal muscles and parts of the dermis.

notes.A: Splanchnopleuric mesoderm is the visceral lateral plate layer adjacent to endoderm. It contributes to gut wall and other visceral structures.
notes.B: Somatopleuric mesoderm lies beside ectoderm as part of the body wall. It does not segment into paired somites.
notes.C: Lateral plate mesoderm divides into two layers around the developing body cavity. Somites are positioned closer to the midline.
notes.D: Intermediate mesoderm contributes renal and reproductive structures and lies lateral to the somite-forming territory.

ana-emb-sa-i-1.why: Sacrococcygeal teratomas are classically attributed to persistent pluripotent cells in the caudal primitive streak region. Their location and mixture of tissues fit an early embryonic remnant.

notes.A: The notochord is associated with chordoma, a distinct tumour. It is not the classical source of sacrococcygeal teratoma.
notes.B: The primitive knot is the cranial node of the streak. The classical origin refers to remnants in the caudal streak region.
notes.D: Mesenchyme can contribute components within a teratoma. It does not identify the pluripotent embryonic remnant implied by the lesion.
notes.E: The prechordal plate lies toward the head and helps organise cranial development. The tumour is centred at the caudal midline.

ana-emb-sa-i-10.why: The notochord forms a central axial rod beneath the neural plate. It supplies signalling and structural landmarks around which adjacent tissues organise on either side of the midline.

notes.A: The prechordal plate helps organise structures at the cranial end. The notochord provides a longitudinal midline along much of the embryo.
notes.B: The cloacal membrane marks the caudal outlet region. It does not act as the longitudinal axial organiser.
notes.C: The oropharyngeal membrane defines the future oral opening. It is a local cranial boundary rather than the main axial rod.
notes.D: Intraembryonic mesoderm gives rise to several regions. Its central axial component forms the specific midline structure asked for.

ana-emb-es-48.why: The brain develops from the cranial neural tube. Closure establishes this tube from neuroectoderm, and subsequent expansion into brain vesicles helps drive the embryo’s cephalic curvature.

notes.A: Mesoderm forms supporting tissues and contributes to embryonic folding. The brain itself develops from cranial neuroectoderm.
notes.C: Lateral folding helps close the ventral body wall and incorporate gut endoderm. It does not establish the cranial neural tube.
notes.D: Amniotic expansion changes the space surrounding the embryo. It does not generate the tissue that becomes brain.
notes.E: Endoderm gives rise to internal epithelial structures, including the gut lining. Brain tissue forms from the neural plate.

ana-emb-es-81.why: The upper urinary tract develops largely from intermediate mesoderm, including the nephron and collecting system primordia. Endoderm of the urogenital sinus supplies much of the lower urinary lining.

notes.A: Ectoderm is not a principal source of the main urinary tract epithelia or renal tissue in this classification.
notes.B: Endoderm supplies much of the bladder and urethral epithelium. Mesoderm also contributes the kidneys and urinary collecting structures.
notes.C: Intermediate mesoderm supplies the upper urinary tract. The lower tract also has an endodermal epithelial contribution.
notes.D: Neural crest contributes peripheral neural components. It does not supply the main epithelial and renal primordia asked for here.

ana-emb-es-87.why: The intraembryonic coelom forms within lateral plate mesoderm. It is the common early cavity that is subsequently partitioned into pericardial, pleural and peritoneal spaces.

notes.A: The amniotic cavity surrounds the embryo externally. It does not become an internal thoracic or abdominal body cavity.
notes.B: The chorionic cavity is the extraembryonic coelom. The internal body cavities form from a separate intraembryonic space.
notes.D: The yolk sac is an extraembryonic endoderm-lined sac connected to the developing gut. It is not an internal coelom.
notes.E: The pericardial cavity develops from the cranial part of the coelom. It is one subdivision of the primordial cavity.

ana-emb-es-88.why: Spaces coalesce within lateral plate mesoderm to form the intraembryonic coelom. This divides lateral plate into somatic and splanchnic layers on either side of the space.

notes.A: Paraxial mesoderm lies next to the neural tube and forms somites. The coelom develops farther laterally.
notes.B: Intermediate mesoderm contains nephrogenic precursors. The internal coelomic cleft opens in lateral plate mesoderm.
notes.D: Neural crest cells migrate from the developing neural tube. They do not form the mesodermal layers around this cavity.
notes.E: The primitive node is a gastrulation organiser. It supplies axial progenitors rather than being the site of coelomic cavitation.

ana-emb-es-90.why: The septum transversum forms a partial partition after head folding. Paired pericardioperitoneal canals remain alongside the foregut and connect the developing thoracic and abdominal coelomic regions.

notes.B: Pleuropericardial folds later partition the pleural and pericardial cavities. The early openings connect toward the peritoneal coelom.
notes.C: Pleuroperitoneal communication describes the later passage between pleural and peritoneal spaces that closes during diaphragmatic development.
notes.D: The peritoneal cavity is the abdominal space itself. The openings beside the septum are narrow connecting passages.
notes.E: The pleural cavities develop as lung buds expand into the canal regions. The original openings have a different anatomical name.

ana-emb-es-93.why: In the classical embryological account, the septum transversum supplies the central tendon of the diaphragm. It forms a ventral partition that later joins developing posterior components.

notes.A: The dorsal oesophageal mesentery gives rise to the crura near the oesophageal hiatus, away from the main central tendon.
notes.B: The lateral body wall supplies mesenchyme for the peripheral diaphragm as the partition enlarges.
notes.C: Cervical somites provide muscle precursors to the diaphragm. The central tendon is the connective tissue component specified here.
notes.D: Pleuroperitoneal membranes close posterolateral communications and join the other developing diaphragmatic components.

ana-emb-es-112.why: The spleen develops from mesenchyme within the dorsal mesogastrium. Foregut endoderm contributes epithelial structures such as the oesophageal lining, respiratory epithelium and gallbladder lining.

notes.A: The oesophageal lining is derived from dorsal foregut endoderm. Its muscular and connective tissue layers have additional origins.
notes.B: Tracheal epithelium forms from the ventral foregut respiratory diverticulum. Adjacent mesoderm supplies supporting structures.
notes.C: The lung buds arise from ventral foregut. Their endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the branching respiratory tree.
notes.E: The gallbladder forms from the cystic portion of the hepatic diverticulum, a ventral foregut endodermal outgrowth.
